key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Elsinore. A platform before the castle.|1|1
summary: At midnight, Bernardo relieves Francisco, who is cold and troubled but says his watch has been quiet. Marcellus and Horatio arrive, and Marcellus explains that he has brought the skeptical Horatio to see and speak to a frightening apparition that the guards have seen twice; Bernardo says he has seen nothing tonight.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Elsinore. A platform before the castle.|4|481
summary: Horatio fears that the appearance of the dead king’s ghost signals trouble for Denmark. Marcellus asks why the country is mounting nightly watches and urgently preparing for war, and Horatio explains that the late King Hamlet killed Norway’s Fortinbras in a duel, winning his lands under an agreement in which Hamlet had also risked his own lands.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Elsinore. A platform before the castle.|5|641
summary: Horatio explains that the former king of Norway lost his life and lands to King Hamlet, and that young Fortinbras has gathered a band of lawless men to reclaim the lands by force. Horatio believes this is why Denmark is preparing for war. Bernardo agrees and connects the appearance of the armed ghost, which resembles the dead King Hamlet, to the conflict; Horatio finds it troubling.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Elsinore. A platform before the castle.|3|321
summary: Horatio orders a ghost resembling the dead king to speak, but it walks away without answering, leaving him pale and shaken. He says its armor and frown recall the king in battle, while Marcellus reports seeing it twice before; Horatio fears it signals trouble for Denmark, and Marcellus asks why the nightly watch is so strict.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Elsinore. A platform before the castle.|2|161
summary: Marcellus brings Horatio to the night watch to witness and speak to an apparition, but Horatio doubts it will appear. As Bernardo begins recounting what he and Marcellus saw, the apparition returns looking like the dead king; Horatio is frightened and amazed, and demands that it speak, but it seems offended and walks away.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|1|1
summary: King Claudius says that although the kingdom still mourns his brother, he has married his former sister-in-law, balancing grief with joy, and thanks his advisers for their support. He also says that young Fortinbras believes Denmark is weak and has repeatedly demanded the return of lands his father lost to Claudius’s brother.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Elsinore. A platform before the castle.|7|961
summary: Horatio urges the ghost to speak, asking whether he can help it, whether it knows Denmark’s fate, or whether it has buried treasure. When the ghost leaves, Marcellus regrets threatening to strike such a majestic figure, whose body cannot be harmed. Bernardo says it was about to speak when the cock crowed, and Horatio says the sound sends wandering spirits back to their places.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Elsinore. A platform before the castle.|9|1281
summary: Horatio is convinced that the spirit, which has not spoken to them, will speak to Hamlet. He asks whether they should tell Hamlet about it out of affection and duty, and Marcellus agrees, saying he knows where to find Hamlet that morning.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|4|481
summary: King Claudius gives Laertes permission to leave, then asks why Hamlet still seems unhappy. Hamlet privately resents his closeness to Claudius, while Queen Gertrude urges him to stop mourning his father, since everyone must die. Hamlet insists that his grief is real and deeper than his black clothes, tears, and other outward signs can show.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|3|321
summary: King Claudius asks Laertes what he wants, and Laertes requests permission to return to France after attending the coronation. Polonius says he reluctantly agreed after much persuasion, and Claudius grants the request. When Claudius addresses Hamlet as his relative and son, Hamlet privately remarks that they are too closely related and not genuinely friendly.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Elsinore. A platform before the castle.|8|1121
summary: Horatio says the ghost’s disappearance confirms that wandering spirits retreat when the rooster crows. Marcellus recalls a belief that at Christmas, spirits cannot roam and magic cannot harm anyone. As dawn breaks, Horatio proposes ending their watch and telling Prince Hamlet about the ghost, confident it will speak to him; Marcellus agrees.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|2|161
summary: King Claudius says young Fortinbras has repeatedly demanded the return of lands his father lost to Claudius’s brother. Claudius sends Cornelius and Voltimand to ask Fortinbras’s bedridden uncle, the king of Norway, to stop him, limiting their authority and urging haste. After they pledge their duty and leave, Claudius invites Laertes to make his request.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Elsinore. A platform before the castle.|6|801
summary: Bernardo says the armed figure looks like the dead king and may be connected to the wars. Horatio finds it troubling and recalls strange signs before Julius Caesar fell, as well as similar warnings in Denmark. When the ghost returns, Horatio risks confronting it and asks it to speak if he can help it; a rooster crows as he begins another question.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|5|641
summary: Hamlet says that his sorrow is deeper than his sad expression and other outward signs of grief, which anyone could pretend to show. King Claudius praises Hamlet for mourning his father but says that continued grief is stubborn, unmanly, and contrary to heaven and reason, since all fathers must eventually die.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|6|801
summary: King Claudius tells Hamlet that continued grief for his dead father is unreasonable and asks him to regard Claudius as a loving father and heir to the throne. Claudius and Queen Gertrude urge Hamlet to stay in Denmark rather than return to school in Wittenberg; Hamlet agrees to obey his mother, and Claudius welcomes his answer.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|10|1441
summary: Hamlet imagines his dead father and praises him as a man whose equal he will never see again. Horatio says he believes he saw the king the previous night and describes how Marcellus and Bernardo saw an armed figure resembling him on two nights, leaving them too frightened to speak. Horatio then joined them on watch the third night.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|9|1281
summary: Hamlet warmly greets Horatio and Marcellus and asks why Horatio has left Wittenberg for Elsinore, rejecting Horatio’s claim that he is playing truant. Horatio says he came for Hamlet’s father’s funeral, but Hamlet bitterly notes that his mother’s wedding followed so quickly that the funeral food could have served both occasions. Grieving and distressed, Hamlet says he can see his father in his mind.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|8|1121
summary: Hamlet bitterly recalls how his mother, Gertrude, seemed devoted to his father but married his uncle within a month of the funeral. He condemns the marriage and its speed, fears it cannot end well, and decides he must keep silent. Horatio greets Hamlet, who calls him a friend, asks why he has left Wittenberg, and recognizes Marcellus.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|11|1601
summary: Horatio tells Hamlet that terrified guards saw an apparition, and that he later saw it himself and recognized Hamlet’s father. Marcellus says it appeared on the watch platform, and Horatio says it seemed ready to speak but vanished when a rooster crowed. Troubled, Hamlet asks whether the guards will watch again that night and whether they will be armed.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|12|1761
summary: Troubled by Horatio’s report, Hamlet questions him, Marcellus, and Bernardo about the armed ghost of his father. Horatio says its exposed face was pale and sorrowful, its gaze steady, and its beard dark streaked with gray. Hamlet decides to join the watch and speak to the ghost despite any danger, and asks the men to keep the sight and anything that happens that night secret.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|13|1921
summary: Hamlet asks his companions to keep the sight they have witnessed secret and to say nothing about whatever happens that night. He thanks them and promises to meet them on the platform between eleven and twelve. Alone, he worries that his father’s spirit appearing in armor signals foul play, and believes that hidden wrongdoing will eventually come to light.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A room of state in the castle.|7|961
summary: King Claudius welcomes Hamlet’s willing agreement and says cannon fire will mark the royal toasts. Alone, Hamlet wishes he could melt away or that God did not forbid suicide, and he sees the world as corrupt and worthless. He mourns his father, praises his love for Hamlet’s mother, and painfully recalls how devoted she seemed to him.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Polonius' house.|1|1
summary: Laertes tells his sister Ophelia that his belongings are aboard ship and asks her to write to him; she wonders whether he doubts she will. He warns her that Hamlet’s affection may be brief and urges her to be cautious, because Hamlet’s royal position means his choice of a partner must serve the state rather than his own wishes.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Polonius' house.|2|161
summary: Laertes tells his sister Ophelia that Hamlet’s choice of a wife must be approved by Denmark, so she should be cautious about believing his declarations of love. He warns her to guard her honor and resist desire, saying that youth is vulnerable to temptation and slander; Ophelia promises to remember his advice.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Polonius' house.|4|481
summary: Polonius advises Laertes to value proven friends, avoid quarrels, listen more than he speaks, dress well without being flashy, and neither borrow nor lend money. He urges Laertes to be true to himself, gives him his blessing, and tells him it is time to leave. Laertes says goodbye to Ophelia and asks her to remember his advice; she assures him that she does.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Polonius' house.|3|321
summary: Laertes warns Ophelia that youth is vulnerable to danger, and she promises to remember his advice while urging him to follow it himself. Polonius arrives and tells Laertes to hurry aboard his ship, giving him his blessing and advice. He urges Laertes to guard his words and actions, keep proven friends close, be cautious with new acquaintances, and avoid quarrels.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Polonius' house.|6|801
summary: Ophelia tells her father, Polonius, that Hamlet has courted her honorably and supported his declarations of love with solemn vows, but she does not know what to think. Polonius calls her naive, warns that Hamlet’s promises may be traps fueled by fleeting passion, and tells her to be less available to him because he has more freedom than she does.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Polonius' house.|7|961
summary: Polonius warns Ophelia that Hamlet has more freedom than she does and that his vows disguise improper intentions. He orders her not to believe Hamlet’s promises or spend any time talking with him, and Ophelia says she will obey.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Polonius' house.|5|641
summary: Laertes takes his leave of Polonius and reminds Ophelia to remember his advice; she promises she will. Polonius asks what Laertes said and questions Ophelia about her private meetings with Hamlet and his declarations of affection. When she admits she does not know what to think, Polonius calls her naive for believing Hamlet’s promises.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  The platform.|1|1
summary: On a bitterly cold night, Hamlet tells Horatio that midnight has struck, and Horatio realizes it is nearly time for the spirit to appear. When trumpets and cannon sound, Hamlet explains that the king is drinking and celebrating; he condemns the custom for giving Denmark a reputation for drunkenness and diminishing its achievements, comparing it to a natural flaw in a person.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  The platform.|3|321
summary: Hamlet addresses the ghost of his father, asking why it has risen from the grave in armor and what he should do. Horatio and Marcellus say the ghost is beckoning Hamlet to follow it somewhere private, but warn him not to go. Hamlet decides to follow, saying he places little value on his life and questioning what the ghost can do to his soul.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  The platform.|2|161
summary: Hamlet says that a single flaw, whether inborn or acquired, can damage a person’s reputation and obscure even great virtues and achievements. Horatio announces the arrival of a ghost, and Hamlet calls on angels for protection before addressing it as his father, the former king, and urgently begging it to answer him.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  The platform.|4|481
summary: Hamlet says he will follow the silent ghost, declaring that he values his life little and believes his immortal soul is safe. Horatio fears the ghost might lead him to the sea or a cliff, take a terrifying shape, and drive him mad. When Horatio and Marcellus try to stop him, Hamlet insists that fate is calling him and threatens to kill anyone who holds him back.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  The platform.|5|641
summary: Hamlet says he feels strong and fearless, threatens to kill anyone who stops him, and follows the ghost. Horatio fears that Hamlet’s imagination is driving him to desperate action, while Marcellus says that something is wrong in Denmark; despite Hamlet’s orders, they decide to follow him, trusting that heaven will guide events.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Another part of the platform.|1|1
summary: Hamlet asks where the ghost is leading him and refuses to go farther. The ghost says it is his father’s spirit, condemned to walk at night and suffer in fire by day until its sins are purged; it asks Hamlet to listen and avenge his father’s murder, leaving him shocked.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Another part of the platform.|2|161
summary: The ghost of Hamlet’s father tells Hamlet that he was murdered and demands revenge. Hamlet is shocked but eager to act, and the ghost reveals that the story of a snake killing him was a lie: Hamlet’s uncle killed him and now wears his crown. The ghost bitterly describes how the uncle used his charm and gifts to seduce the queen.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Another part of the platform.|3|321
summary: The Ghost tells Hamlet that his uncle used cunning and gifts to seduce the queen, whom the Ghost believed virtuous, and bitterly contrasts his own faithful love with her lust. Sensing morning approaching, he says Hamlet’s uncle poured poison into his ear while he slept in his orchard, causing it to race through his body and curdle his blood.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Another part of the platform.|4|481
summary: The Ghost tells Hamlet that a poison raced through his blood and covered his body with a foul crust, killing him as he slept. He says his brother took his life, crown, and queen, leaving him to die with sins unconfessed and without last rites. He urges Hamlet to act, but not to harm his mother, and says goodbye as dawn approaches.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Another part of the platform.|5|641
summary: The ghost tells Hamlet to leave his mother to heaven and her guilty conscience, then says goodbye as dawn approaches and asks Hamlet to remember him. Shaken and angry, Hamlet vows to erase everything else from his memory and keep the ghost’s command, condemning his mother and writing that his smiling uncle is a villain.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Another part of the platform.|7|961
summary: Hamlet suggests that he and his friends part, saying he will go pray. When Horatio calls his words strange, Hamlet says the ghost is honest and asks Horatio and Marcellus not to reveal what they have seen; they agree, but he insists they swear on his sword. The ghost calls from beneath them to swear, and Horatio asks Hamlet to state the oath.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Another part of the platform.|6|801
summary: Hamlet writes that a smiling man can be a villain, thinking of his uncle, and recalls his promise to remember the ghost. When Horatio and Marcellus find him, he says he has wonderful news but fears they will reveal it; after they promise secrecy, he offers a vague remark about villains and suggests they part.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Another part of the platform.|8|1121
summary: Hamlet asks Horatio and Marcellus to swear on his sword never to reveal what they have seen or heard, while the ghost repeatedly calls on them to swear from beneath the ground. Horatio is amazed, and Hamlet says there are things beyond human understanding; he also asks them not to hint at what they know if he later acts strangely.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  A room in POLONIUS' house.|1|1
summary: Polonius tells Reynaldo to deliver money and letters to his son, but first to ask Danes in Paris about the son’s behavior and companions. He instructs Reynaldo to pretend he barely knows the young man and suggest minor misconduct, such as gambling, drinking, fighting, or visiting prostitutes, without making accusations serious enough to disgrace him.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Another part of the platform.|9|1281
summary: Hamlet tells his companions that he may pretend to be mad and makes them swear not to hint that they know anything about him. The Ghost calls from below for them to swear, and Hamlet tells the troubled spirit to rest. After they swear, Hamlet promises his friendship, asks them to remain silent, and laments that he was born to set a troubled world right.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  A room in POLONIUS' house.|2|161
summary: Polonius tells Reynaldo to mention minor faults such as gambling, drinking, and quarrelling when speaking about his son Laertes, but not to accuse him of anything seriously dishonorable. When Reynaldo questions the plan, Polonius explains that these suggestions may encourage someone who has seen Laertes behave badly to admit what they know.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  A room in POLONIUS' house.|4|481
summary: Polonius tells Reynaldo to observe his son’s behavior and encourage him to practice music, then sends him away. Ophelia enters frightened and describes how Hamlet came into her room looking disheveled, pale, trembling, and miserable, then gripped her wrist. When Polonius asks whether Hamlet is mad with love for her, she says she does not know but fears he is.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  A room in POLONIUS' house.|3|321
summary: Polonius tells Reynaldo that people who have seen his son misbehave may confirm the accusations Reynaldo makes, mentioning gambling, drunkenness, arguments at tennis, or visits to a brothel. When Polonius loses his train of thought, Reynaldo reminds him where he stopped, and Polonius explains that falsehood can be used to uncover the truth.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  A room in POLONIUS' house.|5|641
summary: Ophelia tells Polonius that Hamlet gripped her wrist, studied her face, shook her arm, and sighed deeply before leaving while still staring at her. She fears he has gone mad with love for her. Polonius agrees, regrets his distress, and decides to seek the king, saying that love can drive people to desperate acts.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  A room in POLONIUS' house.|6|801
summary: Polonius says that Hamlet’s intense love may drive him to desperate actions and asks Ophelia whether she has spoken harshly to him. She says she rejected Hamlet’s letters and refused to see him as Polonius ordered; Polonius blames this for Hamlet’s madness, regrets doubting his intentions, and decides they must tell the king.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|1|1
summary: King Claudius welcomes Rosencrantz and Guildenstern and asks them to stay at court, cheer up their old friend Hamlet, and discover what might be troubling him beyond his father’s death. Queen Gertrude says Hamlet often speaks of them and is deeply attached to them, and she also asks them to stay.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|6|801
summary: Polonius tells Queen Gertrude that his obedient daughter Ophelia has shown him a letter, and Gertrude asks whether it came from Hamlet. Polonius reads Hamlet’s declaration of love, criticizes some of its wording, and says Ophelia has also told him about Hamlet’s advances. King Claudius begins to ask how she responded.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|3|321
summary: Polonius assures King Claudius of his loyalty and says he has discovered the cause of Hamlet’s apparent madness, but suggests hearing the ambassadors first. Queen Gertrude suspects Hamlet is distressed by his father’s death and her hasty marriage. Voltimand reports that the king of Norway tried to stop his nephew’s military preparations after discovering they were aimed at Denmark, not Poland.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|2|161
summary: Queen Gertrude asks Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to spend time at court and visit her much-changed son, Hamlet, promising the king’s thanks. They offer their services, and Guildenstern hopes their visit will help Hamlet. Polonius announces that the ambassadors from Norway have returned, then assures King Claudius of his loyalty to God and the king.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|5|641
summary: King Claudius thanks someone for their work, welcomes them home, and promises a feast that night. Polonius tells Claudius and Queen Gertrude that their son Hamlet is mad; when Gertrude asks him to get to the point, he says they must find the cause and begins to speak of his daughter.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|4|481
summary: Voltimand reports that the king of Norway discovered his nephew Fortinbras had raised troops against Denmark, made him promise not to attack, and gave him money and permission to fight Poland instead. Norway requests safe passage through Denmark; King Claudius welcomes the news, promises to consider the request, and invites Voltimand to a feast, while Polonius considers the matter well settled.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|7|961
summary: Polonius tells King Claudius that his daughter Ophelia showed him Hamlet’s letter and described his attempts to court her. When Claudius asks how she responded, Polonius says he warned her that Hamlet was above her station and told her to refuse his visits, messages, and gifts; rejected, Hamlet became sad and stopped eating.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|8|1121
summary: Polonius tells King Claudius and Queen Gertrude that his daughter Ophelia rejected Hamlet on his advice, causing Hamlet to become depressed and eventually go mad. Gertrude thinks this is likely, and Polonius confidently proposes a test: he and Claudius can hide and watch Hamlet meet Ophelia to see whether love has driven him mad.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|9|1281
summary: Polonius proposes letting his daughter meet Hamlet while he and King Claudius hide and watch, to test whether love has driven Hamlet mad. Claudius agrees, and Queen Gertrude notices Hamlet approaching sadly with a book. After they leave, Polonius speaks to Hamlet, who calls him a fishmonger, says honesty is rare, and warns him to guard his daughter against pregnancy. Polonius notes that Hamlet is still talking about her.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|12|1761
summary: Hamlet warmly greets Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, who joke that fortune has treated them moderately well. Hamlet calls Denmark a prison, though his friends disagree; he says that a person’s thinking determines whether something is good or bad. Rosencrantz suggests that Hamlet feels confined because his ambition is too great for Denmark.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|10|1441
summary: Hamlet warns Polonius to watch his daughter, hinting that she might become pregnant. Polonius privately thinks Hamlet is mad with love, though he notices a method in his madness. Asked what he is reading, Hamlet mocks old men as wrinkled, weak and foolish, and Polonius asks him to come in out of the air.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|11|1601
summary: Hamlet jokes that Polonius could become younger by walking backward and responds to an invitation to leave the air by mentioning his grave. Polonius privately sees sense in Hamlet’s apparent madness and plans to arrange a meeting with his daughter. After Polonius leaves, Hamlet calls him a tedious fool and warmly greets Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, who say their fortunes are moderate.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|15|2241
summary: Hamlet presses Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to admit whether they were sent for, and Guildenstern confirms that they were. Hamlet says he has lost his happiness and given up his usual activities; the earth and sky seem bleak and foul to him, and although he praises humanity’s remarkable qualities, he finds no pleasure in them.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|14|2081
summary: Hamlet asks Rosencrantz and Guildenstern why they have come to Elsinore, and Rosencrantz says they only came to visit him. Suspecting that the king and queen sent for them, Hamlet appeals to their lifelong friendship and asks for an honest answer. Rosencrantz quietly asks Guildenstern what to say, and Hamlet notices their hesitation.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|13|1921
summary: Hamlet says Denmark feels like a prison to him and that bad dreams keep him from feeling free, while Rosencrantz and Guildenstern suggest his ambition is to blame. After they trade thoughts about dreams, ambition, and shadows, Hamlet asks why they have come to Elsinore. Rosencrantz says they came only to visit him, and Hamlet thanks them, though he says he has little gratitude to offer.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|16|2401
summary: Hamlet praises human beauty and intelligence but says that neither men nor women delight him. Rosencrantz explains that he smiled because he wondered how Hamlet would welcome the actors now approaching the castle. Hamlet says he will welcome their various characters and asks who the actors are; Rosencrantz says they are the city’s tragedians, whom Hamlet used to enjoy.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|19|2881
summary: Hamlet suggests that something supernatural is happening, then formally welcomes Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to Elsinore. He says his uncle and mother are mistaken about him, claiming that he is mad only sometimes and can still tell things apart. Hamlet mocks Polonius as a baby and correctly predicts that he has come to announce the actors.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|17|2561
summary: Hamlet says the lady will speak freely, even if the poetry suffers, and asks why his favorite city actors are now traveling. Rosencrantz says they are less popular because fashionable child actors mock the ordinary theaters and draw enthusiastic applause. Hamlet asks who pays the children and wonders what they will think of their writers if they later become ordinary actors themselves.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|20|3041
summary: Polonius tells Hamlet that actors have arrived and praises their ability to perform every kind of play, while Hamlet interrupts him with jokes. Hamlet calls Polonius Jephthah and speaks of his beloved daughter; Polonius thinks Hamlet is referring to his own daughter and admits he loves her. Hamlet dismisses his answer and points out the arriving actors.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|21|3201
summary: Hamlet greets a group of actors warmly, teasing one about his new beard and a younger performer about growing taller and possibly having a broken voice. He asks them for an emotional speech from a play he remembers admiring, though it was performed rarely because it did not appeal to the general public.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|18|2721
summary: Hamlet asks how the boy actors are paid and whether they will resent writers who make them mock adult actors if they later join them. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern describe the fierce rivalry between the acting companies, saying the boys are winning. Hamlet compares this change in popularity to people paying for portraits of his uncle, whom they once mocked, and welcomes the others to Elsinore.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|22|3361
summary: Hamlet recalls a play that was unpopular with the public but that he and other discerning people considered excellent, praising its skillful, straightforward writing. He asks an actor to recite his favorite speech, in which Aeneas tells Dido about Priam’s killing, and tries to remember its opening lines about Pyrrhus in black armor.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|23|3521
summary: Hamlet recites a speech describing the blood-covered Greek warrior Pyrrhus searching for the elderly King Priam amid the burning city of Troy. Polonius praises Hamlet’s delivery, and the First Player continues: Priam struggles to fight, falls as Pyrrhus attacks, and hears the city crash as Pyrrhus’s sword descends toward his head.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|24|3681
summary: The First Player describes burning Troy collapsing as Pyrrhus pauses before striking the elderly Priam, then renews his attack in a fury. He curses Fortune and calls on the gods to destroy her power. Polonius complains that the speech is too long, but Hamlet mocks his beard and his taste for jigs and dirty stories, then asks the player to continue.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|25|3841
summary: Polonius complains that the First Player’s speech is too long, but Hamlet mocks him and asks the player to continue. The player describes Queen Hecuba fleeing in fear and crying out as Pyrrhus cuts up her husband’s body, a sight that could move the gods to tears. Noticing the player’s own tears, Polonius asks him to stop; Hamlet says he will hear the rest later.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|29|4481
summary: Hamlet angrily curses his uncle and reproaches himself for talking about revenge for his father’s murder instead of acting. He plans to have actors perform a scene like the murder and watch his uncle’s reaction for signs of guilt. Hamlet fears that the spirit he saw might be a devil deceiving him, so he wants stronger proof.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|27|4161
summary: Hamlet asks the First Player to perform The Murder of Gonzago the next night and learn a short speech Hamlet will write, then sends him away and dismisses Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. Alone, Hamlet criticizes himself, marveling that the actor wept for Hecuba and imagining how powerfully he would perform if he had Hamlet’s own reasons for grief.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|26|4001
summary: Polonius stops the First Player’s moving speech, noticing that he has changed color and has tears in his eyes. Hamlet asks Polonius to treat the players generously, saying their words can shape people’s reputations. He then arranges for them to perform The Murder of Gonzago the next night and asks the First Player to learn a speech he will add to it.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|30|4641
summary: Hamlet worries that the spirit he has seen may be the devil in a pleasing form, taking advantage of his weakness and sadness to deceive and damn him. He decides to use a play to test the king’s conscience and obtain more reliable evidence.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  A room in the castle.|28|4321
summary: Hamlet wonders how an actor can weep for Hecuba and imagines the powerful performance he would give if he had Hamlet’s reason for grief. He calls himself a coward for failing to avenge his murdered father, imagines himself accepting insults without resistance, and angrily denounces his father’s killer.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|1|1
summary: King Claudius and Queen Gertrude ask Rosencrantz and Guildenstern about Hamlet’s disturbed behavior. The two men say Hamlet admits he is distracted but will not explain why, and that he received them politely, though with some effort. Rosencrantz says Hamlet was pleased to hear that actors had arrived; Polonius adds that Hamlet has invited the king and queen to their performance, and Claudius gladly agrees.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|3|321
summary: Polonius tells Ophelia to walk and read so that her solitude looks natural, then withdraws with Claudius as Hamlet approaches. His remark that piety can disguise evil troubles Claudius’s guilty conscience. Hamlet wonders whether to endure life’s troubles or end them by dying, imagining death as a welcome sleep but pausing over the possibility of dreams.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|5|641
summary: Hamlet reflects that overthinking makes people fearful and prevents them from acting, then asks Ophelia to remember his sins in her prayers. Ophelia offers to return his gifts, saying they have lost their value because he has become unkind, but Hamlet denies giving her anything and questions whether beauty and honesty can coexist.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|4|481
summary: Hamlet describes death as a welcome end to heartache and life’s many injustices, and wonders why people endure such suffering when they could kill themselves. He concludes that fear of what may follow death makes people bear the troubles they know, while too much thought weakens their resolve to act.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|6|801
summary: Hamlet asks Ophelia whether she is honest and beautiful, arguing that beauty is more likely to corrupt honesty than honesty is to improve beauty. He says he once loved her, then denies it, leaving her feeling deceived. He tells her to enter a convent rather than bear sinners and condemns himself as proud, vengeful, ambitious, and capable of many wrongs.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|2|161
summary: Polonius says Hamlet wants the king and queen to see the entertainment, and Claudius tells the gentlemen to encourage his interest. Claudius asks Gertrude to leave so he and Polonius can secretly watch Hamlet meet Ophelia and judge whether love is causing his distress. Gertrude and Ophelia hope it is, and Polonius tells Ophelia to read a book while she waits.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|7|961
summary: Hamlet calls himself and other men wicked, tells Ophelia to enter a convent, and mocks her father after she says he is at home. He warns that even a virtuous wife will be slandered, advises her to marry a fool if she must marry, and condemns women’s makeup and affected behavior. Ophelia appeals to heaven to help and restore him.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|8|1121
summary: Hamlet condemns women’s makeup and affected behavior, declares that there will be no more marriages, threatens one married person, and tells Ophelia to go to a convent. Ophelia mourns the apparent loss of his noble mind and remembers his loving promises. King Claudius doubts that love or madness explains Hamlet’s behavior and senses that something troubles him.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|9|1281
summary: Ophelia laments the change she sees in Hamlet. King Claudius doubts that love or madness explains Hamlet’s behavior and fears his melancholy may lead to danger, so he decides to send him to England to collect unpaid tribute and distract him. Polonius still believes rejected love is the cause and suggests that Hamlet’s mother question him after the play while Polonius listens.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|1|1
summary: Hamlet advises the First Player to speak his lines naturally, use restrained gestures, and avoid exaggerated displays of passion. The player promises to do so, and Hamlet adds that the acting should not be too restrained either: words and actions should suit each other and reflect nature.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|10|1441
summary: Polonius suggests that after the play, Hamlet’s mother should question him directly about his grief while Polonius secretly listens. If she cannot discover what troubles him, Polonius recommends sending him to England or confining him elsewhere; King Claudius agrees, saying that madness in powerful people must be watched.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|2|161
summary: Hamlet tells the actors to match their actions to their words and perform naturally, because acting should reflect human character and the times. He criticizes actors who strut and shout, saying their performances may amuse the uninformed but upset discerning viewers. When the First Player hopes they have improved, Hamlet urges them to eliminate such faults and tells the clowns to stick to the script.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|3|321
summary: Hamlet tells the actors to improve their performances and warns clowns not to improvise or laugh to prompt the audience, distracting from important parts of the play. Polonius says the king and queen will watch shortly, so Hamlet asks him, Rosencrantz, and Guildenstern to hurry the players. Hamlet then praises Horatio’s honesty, insisting he has no reason to flatter a poor man.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|5|641
summary: Hamlet asks Horatio to watch King Claudius closely during a scene that resembles the reported circumstances of Hamlet’s father’s death. Hamlet says they will compare their impressions to judge whether the king shows guilt, and Horatio agrees. As the others arrive, Hamlet decides to act foolishly, gives Claudius a strange answer, and asks Polonius about acting at university.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|4|481
summary: Hamlet tells Horatio that he is not flattering him for gain, but truly values his ability to accept good and bad fortune without being ruled by emotion. He says he holds Horatio close to his heart, then mentions that a scene in the play before the king resembles the circumstances of his father’s death.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|7|961
summary: Hamlet jokes bitterly about his mother’s cheerfulness after his father’s death and doubts that even a great man will be remembered for long. When a silent performance begins, he tells Ophelia it means mischief and makes a suggestive joke about explaining it; she calls him naughty and decides to watch the play.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|6|801
summary: After Claudius rejects Hamlet’s words, Hamlet jokes about Polonius playing Julius Caesar and learns that the actors are ready. He declines Gertrude’s invitation to sit beside her, asks to rest his head in Ophelia’s lap, and makes sexual jokes. Hamlet remarks bitterly on his mother’s cheerfulness so soon after his father’s death, but Ophelia reminds him that four months have passed.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|8|1121
summary: Hamlet makes a suggestive remark to Ophelia, who calls him naughty and turns her attention to the play. After the prologue asks for a patient hearing, Hamlet jokes that it is as brief as a woman’s love. In the play, the king says he and his queen have been married for thirty years; she hopes for thirty more but fears for his declining health.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|12|1761
summary: The Player Queen hopes that no misfortune will come between her and her husband, but Gertrude thinks she protests too much. Claudius asks whether the play is offensive, and Hamlet calls its poisoning a joke, describing it as a murder in Vienna. Hamlet trades suggestive remarks with Ophelia, then urges Lucianus, the murderer, to begin.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|11|1601
summary: The Player King says that plans are defeated by fate and predicts that the Player Queen will remarry after his death, but she swears terrible suffering on herself if she does. He prepares to sleep, and she wishes him peace. Hamlet questions Gertrude about the play; she thinks the lady protests too much, while Claudius asks whether the story is offensive and Hamlet says it is not.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|10|1441
summary: The Player King says that people often break their resolutions when the strong feelings that inspired them fade, and that joy and grief can quickly turn into each other. He wonders whether love shapes fortune or fortune shapes love, noting that friends desert those who lose their status, and concludes that fate often defeats human plans.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|9|1281
summary: The Player Queen says her great love makes her fearful and insists that marrying again would betray her husband, comparing it to killing him. The Player King says he will soon die and suggests she may find another kind husband, then argues that people often break their promises as their intentions fade; Hamlet remarks bitterly on her words.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|13|1921
summary: Hamlet jokes with Ophelia and urges Lucianus to begin; Lucianus prepares a cursed poison, and Hamlet explains that he poisons Gonzago for his estate and will win his wife. Ophelia notices King Claudius rise, and the queen asks what is wrong; Polonius stops the play as Claudius calls for light and leaves. Hamlet jokes that he could earn a living as an actor, while Horatio teases him about his share.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|14|2081
summary: Hamlet jokes with Horatio about becoming an actor and mocks the king, then says he trusts the ghost’s account after Horatio confirms that he noticed the king’s reaction to the mention of poisoning. Hamlet calls for music, but Guildenstern reports that the king is extremely angry; Hamlet jokes about sending for a doctor, frustrating Guildenstern.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|16|2401
summary: Rosencrantz tells Hamlet that his mother is amazed and wants to speak with him privately before bed, and Hamlet agrees. When Rosencrantz asks what troubles him, Hamlet says he lacks advancement despite the king’s support for his succession; he then accuses Guildenstern of trying to trap him and asks him to play a recorder, but Guildenstern says he cannot.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|15|2241
summary: Guildenstern asks Hamlet to speak plainly and says that his mother is deeply upset. Hamlet jokes that his mind is ill but agrees to hear her message. Rosencrantz says that Hamlet’s behavior has astonished the queen and that she wants to speak with him privately before he goes.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|17|2561
summary: Hamlet repeatedly asks Guildenstern to play a pipe, but Guildenstern says he lacks the skill, even after Hamlet explains how to use it. Hamlet angrily compares himself to the pipe, accusing Guildenstern of trying to uncover his secrets and manipulate him. He declares that Guildenstern may annoy him, but cannot control him.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|18|2721
summary: Hamlet tells someone that, although they can irritate him, they cannot manipulate him like a musical instrument. Polonius says the queen wants to see Hamlet immediately, then agrees with each of Hamlet’s changing descriptions of a cloud. After Polonius and the others leave, Hamlet speaks of the night’s evil and his own violent feelings, but urges himself not to be cruel when he visits his mother.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|19|2881
summary: Hamlet feels capable of shocking violence, but as he prepares to see his mother, he urges himself not to become cruel enough to harm her. He resolves to speak to her as sharply as if his words were daggers, while refusing to turn those words into actions.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  A room in the castle.|3|321
summary: King Claudius struggles to decide what to do and wonders whether heaven can forgive him for murdering his brother. He doubts he can be forgiven while keeping the crown and queen he gained through the murder, and he reflects that, unlike earthly justice, divine justice cannot be bribed or deceived.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  A room in the castle.|1|1
summary: King Claudius tells Rosencrantz and Guildenstern that Hamlet’s madness threatens his safety and orders them to prepare to take Hamlet to England. Guildenstern agrees that protecting the king protects his people, while Rosencrantz argues that a king’s downfall brings ruin to everyone who depends on him. Claudius urges them to prepare for the journey quickly.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  A room in the castle.|2|161
summary: Rosencrantz says a king’s troubles affect everyone, and he and Guildenstern agree to make the journey Claudius orders to contain a threat. Polonius plans to hide and overhear Hamlet’s conversation with his mother, then report to the king. Alone, Claudius admits killing his brother and feels too guilty to pray, though he wonders whether his guilt can be washed away.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  A room in the castle.|4|481
summary: King Claudius says that no one can hide their sins from heaven, but he feels trapped because he cannot repent. He calls on angels for help and urges himself to kneel and soften his heart. Hamlet considers killing Claudius as he prays, but questions whether sending him to heaven would avenge his father, who died burdened with sins.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|4|481
summary: Hamlet praises Queen Gertrude’s former husband as godlike and contrasts him with her present husband, whom he describes as corrupting his good brother. He angrily questions how she could prefer the second man, dismisses love as an excuse, and accuses her of being shamefully blind to the difference.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  A room in the castle.|5|641
summary: Hamlet reflects that his father died burdened with sins, while Claudius seems ready for heaven as he prays. He decides not to kill Claudius yet, but to wait until he is sinning so that his soul will go to hell; then Hamlet leaves to see his mother. Rising, Claudius admits that his prayers are empty because his thoughts are not sincere.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|2|161
summary: Gertrude fears Hamlet will murder her and calls for help; when Polonius answers from behind a curtain, Hamlet stabs him, thinking he might be the king. Gertrude is horrified, but Hamlet compares the killing to murdering a king and marrying his brother. He tells Gertrude he intends to make her feel remorse, and she asks what she has done to deserve his accusations.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|1|1
summary: Polonius urges Queen Gertrude to scold Hamlet for his behavior and hides as Hamlet arrives. Gertrude accuses Hamlet of offending his father, but Hamlet says she has offended his father by marrying her husband’s brother and insists she face her own wrongdoing. Fearing murder, Gertrude cries for help; Polonius calls out from hiding, and Hamlet draws his weapon and attacks him.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|3|321
summary: Queen Gertrude asks why Hamlet speaks so rudely to her. Hamlet condemns an unnamed act that he says destroys modesty, makes marriage vows false, and sickens the world. When Gertrude asks what act he means, he shows her pictures of two brothers, praising her former husband’s godlike appearance before pointing to her present husband.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|7|961
summary: Queen Gertrude is alarmed by Hamlet’s agitation and urges him to calm down. Hamlet sees his father’s ghost and fears its pitying gaze will weaken his resolve, but Gertrude can neither see nor hear it. After Hamlet watches the ghost leave, Gertrude calls it a product of his imagination, while Hamlet insists he is sane.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|5|641
summary: Hamlet angrily shames Queen Gertrude for her sexual relationship with Claudius, calling him a murderer, a thief who stole the crown, and a far lesser man than her former husband. Gertrude begs Hamlet to stop, saying his words wound her and reveal stains on her soul; when the Ghost appears, Hamlet cries out for protection.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|6|801
summary: Hamlet calls the king a thief who stole the crown, then sees his father’s ghost and asks whether it has come to rebuke him for delaying its command. The ghost urges him to remember his purpose and comfort his distressed mother. Gertrude, seeing no one, thinks Hamlet is mad and asks him to calm down, but he points to the pale ghost.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|10|1441
summary: When Gertrude asks what she should do, Hamlet sarcastically warns her not to let the king coax her into revealing that his madness is an act. Gertrude promises to keep his secret, then remembers that Hamlet is to go to England. Hamlet mentions sealed letters and his two schoolfellows.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|9|1281
summary: Hamlet tells Queen Gertrude to avoid the king’s bed, saying that doing the right thing will become easier with practice. He regrets killing Polonius but believes heaven has made him an instrument of punishment; he promises to take care of the body and answer for the death. He says he must be cruel to be kind and warns that worse is coming.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|8|1121
summary: Hamlet insists that he is speaking rationally and urges Queen Gertrude not to dismiss her wrongdoing as a product of his madness. She says he has broken her heart, and he tells her to repent, avoid his uncle’s bed, and practice virtue, arguing that good behavior can become a habit.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The Queen's closet.|11|1601
summary: Gertrude promises not to reveal what Hamlet has told her and remembers that he is to go to England. Hamlet distrusts the two schoolfellows carrying sealed orders and looks forward to turning their scheme against them. He says he will drag the dead counselor into the next room, mocks his former talkativeness, and bids his mother good night.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|1|1
summary: After sending Rosencrantz and Guildenstern away, Gertrude tells King Claudius that Hamlet, in a violent fit, killed an unseen old man behind a curtain and went to remove the body. Claudius fears Hamlet threatens everyone and that he will be blamed for failing to restrain him; he says love kept him from recognizing the danger.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|2|161
summary: Gertrude tells King Claudius that Hamlet has taken away Polonius’s body and is weeping over the killing, showing feeling despite his madness. Claudius plans to send Hamlet away at dawn and excuse his actions; he orders Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to find Hamlet and bring the body to the chapel, then calls for advice on protecting his reputation.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE II.  Another room in the castle.|1|1
summary: Hamlet says he has hidden the dead body, and Rosencrantz asks where it is so he and Guildenstern can take it to the chapel. Hamlet refuses to tell him and mocks him as a sponge who absorbs the king’s favors until the king squeezes him dry; Rosencrantz insists that Hamlet go with them to the king.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  A room in the castle.|3|321
summary: King Claudius speaks of what is planned and what has been done too soon. He hopes that poisonous rumors spreading across the world will miss his name and do no harm, then urges someone to come away, saying he feels troubled and dismayed.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE II.  Another room in the castle.|2|161
summary: Rosencrantz tells Hamlet that he must reveal where the body is and go with them to the king. Hamlet gives a puzzling answer about the body and the king, dismisses the king as a thing of nothing, and agrees to go to him with a playful call to chase.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  Another room in the castle.|1|1
summary: King Claudius says Hamlet is dangerous but too popular to punish openly, so he plans to send him away while making the decision appear carefully considered. Rosencrantz reports that Hamlet will not reveal where he put Polonius’s body and brings him before the king. Asked where Polonius is, Hamlet says worms are eating him and remarks that kings and beggars alike become food for worms.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  Another room in the castle.|3|321
summary: King Claudius tells Hamlet to prepare for an immediate journey to England, and Hamlet agrees, mockingly calling him “mother” as he says goodbye. Claudius orders Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to get Hamlet aboard without delay. Alone, Claudius reveals that his letters instruct England to kill Hamlet, whom he sees as a disease that must be cured.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  Another room in the castle.|4|481
summary: King Claudius tells England that his official letters demand Hamlet’s immediate death and that the order must not be ignored. He describes Hamlet as a fever raging in his blood and says he cannot be happy until he knows Hamlet has been killed.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  Another room in the castle.|2|161
summary: Hamlet tells King Claudius that kings and beggars alike become food for worms, and jokes that a king can pass through a beggar’s guts. Asked about Polonius, he suggests looking in heaven or hell, then says his body will eventually smell near the lobby stairs. Claudius orders a search and tells Hamlet to leave quickly for England, claiming it is for his safety.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE IV.  A plain in Denmark.|2|161
summary: A captain tells Hamlet that the disputed land is already defended, and Hamlet laments that thousands of lives and great wealth will be spent fighting over something so worthless. After asking Rosencrantz to go ahead, Hamlet reproaches himself for delaying revenge, questions whether cowardice or overthinking is holding him back, and sees the army as an example urging him to act.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE IV.  A plain in Denmark.|1|1
summary: Fortinbras sends his captain to greet the Danish king and confirm that the Norwegian army will march through Denmark with permission. When Hamlet questions the captain, he learns that the army is heading for a nearly worthless piece of Polish land that is already defended. Hamlet says that thousands of soldiers and great expense will not settle such a trivial dispute, which he calls a sickness caused by wealth and peace.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE IV.  A plain in Denmark.|3|321
summary: Hamlet condemns himself for delaying action despite having the cause and means to act after his father’s murder and his mother’s dishonor. He contrasts his hesitation with a prince’s army, whose men risk death over a tiny piece of land for honor, and resolves that from now on his thoughts will be violent or worthless.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Elsinore. A room in the castle.|1|1
summary: Queen Gertrude initially refuses to see Ophelia, but a gentleman describes her distressed, confused behavior, and Horatio warns that her words could provoke dangerous speculation. Gertrude agrees, privately admitting that guilt makes her fear disaster; when Ophelia enters and sings about recognizing a true love, the queen asks what her song means.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Elsinore. A room in the castle.|2|161
summary: Ophelia asks for the queen and sings about a dead lover buried with flowers, prompting the concerned Queen Gertrude to ask what her song means. King Claudius thinks Ophelia is speaking about her father; Ophelia makes a strange remark about an owl, reflects that no one knows what they may become, and begins a song about a girl visiting a man on Valentine’s Day.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Elsinore. A room in the castle.|3|321
summary: Ophelia sings about a young woman who visits a man on Valentine’s Day, loses her virginity and is denied the marriage he promised her. She says she must be patient but weeps at the thought of her father in the cold ground, and says her brother will hear of it. Claudius asks Horatio to watch her closely, blaming her condition on grief over her father’s death.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Elsinore. A room in the castle.|5|641
summary: King Claudius tells Gertrude that the accusations against him are deeply painful, then orders his guards to protect the door. A gentleman warns that Laertes is leading a crowd demanding that he become king, while Gertrude calls them misguided. Laertes bursts in, tells his followers to wait outside, and angrily demands his father, refusing Gertrude’s plea to be calm.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Elsinore. A room in the castle.|6|801
summary: Laertes thanks the Danes and asks them to guard the door, then angrily demands his father from King Claudius. Gertrude urges him to calm down, but he insists his anger proves he is his father’s son. Claudius tells Laertes that his father is dead, and Gertrude says the king did not kill him; Laertes demands the truth and vows revenge, regardless of the consequences.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Elsinore. A room in the castle.|8|1121
summary: Laertes weeps for his sister Ophelia’s madness and vows that someone will pay for it, saying her condition moves him more than a clear call for revenge could. Ophelia sings about a funeral and a false steward, then offers flowers for remembrance and thoughts, along with fennel, columbines, and rue.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Elsinore. A room in the castle.|7|961
summary: Laertes vows revenge for his father’s death but tells King Claudius that he will target only his father’s enemies and embrace his friends. Claudius praises him and insists that he is innocent and grieves for Laertes’s father. When Ophelia enters, Laertes is devastated by his sister’s madness and vows that someone will pay for it.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VI.  Another room in the castle.|1|1
summary: Horatio receives sailors who bring him a letter from Hamlet, and he reads it aloud. Hamlet says pirates chased his ship, and he became their prisoner when he boarded their vessel during the fight; they have treated him kindly, expecting a favor in return. He asks Horatio to help the sailors deliver letters to the king and then come to him quickly.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Elsinore. A room in the castle.|9|1281
summary: Ophelia gives out flowers, says the violets withered when her father died, and sings sadly that he will never return. Laertes sees meaning and beauty in her madness and cries out to God in distress. King Claudius asks Laertes to discuss his grief and choose wise friends to hear and judge between them.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Elsinore. A room in the castle.|10|1441
summary: King Claudius asks the grieving Laertes to choose wise friends to judge whether the king bears any responsibility for his father’s death, promising to surrender his crown and life if found guilty. Laertes agrees but demands an inquiry into the death and the lack of a proper funeral, and Claudius promises punishment for whoever is responsible.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VI.  Another room in the castle.|2|161
summary: Horatio reads a letter from Hamlet, who says the men bringing it treated him mercifully and that he owes them a favor. Hamlet asks Horatio to deliver letters to the king and come to him quickly, promising startling news about Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, who are continuing to England. Horatio tells the men he will arrange delivery so they can lead him to Hamlet.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VII.  Another room in the castle.|1|1
summary: King Claudius asks Laertes to consider him a friend, saying that Hamlet, who killed Laertes’s father, also tried to kill him. Laertes asks why Claudius did not punish Hamlet, and Claudius explains that the queen loves her son deeply and that the public’s affection for Hamlet would turn any action against him back on the king.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Elsinore. A room in the castle.|4|481
summary: Ophelia says good night, and King Claudius asks Horatio to watch her closely, blaming her distress on her father’s death. He tells Queen Gertrude that their troubles are mounting: Hamlet is gone, people are angry about Polonius’s death and secret burial, and Ophelia’s brother has secretly returned and may hear accusations against him. When Gertrude hears a noise, Claudius orders his guards to protect the door.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VII.  Another room in the castle.|2|161
summary: King Claudius tells Laertes that public affection would have turned any punishment he aimed at Hamlet against himself. Laertes mourns his father and his sister’s desperate condition, but vows revenge; Claudius assures him that he, too, has reason to act. A messenger brings letters from Hamlet for the king and queen, and Claudius sends him away and begins reading aloud.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VII.  Another room in the castle.|5|641
summary: King Claudius says that youthful showiness is as fitting as the seriousness of old age, then describes a Norman gentleman whose horsemanship amazed him. Laertes identifies the man as Lamond and praises him highly. Claudius says Lamond praised Laertes’ fencing, especially his skill with a rapier, and claimed that French fencers would be no match for him.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VII.  Another room in the castle.|3|321
summary: A messenger delivers a letter from Hamlet, and King Claudius reads it to Laertes. Hamlet says he has returned alone and will ask to see the king the next day to explain his unexpected return. Claudius and Laertes are puzzled, but Laertes welcomes the chance to confront Hamlet and agrees to follow the king’s advice, provided it does not require making peace.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VII.  Another room in the castle.|4|481
summary: King Claudius tells Laertes that, if Hamlet has returned and abandoned his journey, he will arrange for Hamlet’s death to look like an accident, even to his mother. Laertes agrees to follow Claudius’s plan, especially if he can be the one to kill Hamlet. Claudius says Hamlet envied a skill for which Laertes had been praised.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VII.  Another room in the castle.|6|801
summary: King Claudius tells Laertes that a report praising his fencing skills made Hamlet so envious that he eagerly wanted Laertes to return and fence with him. Claudius then questions Laertes’s love for his father and says that love and the desire to act can fade over time, so people should act while they still want to.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VII.  Another room in the castle.|7|961
summary: Claudius warns that resolve fades with delay and asks Laertes how he will prove his loyalty to his father. Laertes says he would kill Hamlet even in a church. Claudius proposes arranging a fencing match in which Laertes can choose a sharp sword and kill Hamlet; Laertes agrees and says he will coat his sword.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VII.  Another room in the castle.|8|1121
summary: Claudius suggests that Laertes use a sharp sword in a fencing match to avenge his father, and Laertes agrees to poison its tip so that even a scratch could kill Hamlet. Worried that the plot might fail or be exposed, Claudius proposes a backup involving a wager, a vigorous match, and a cup prepared for Hamlet when he asks for a drink.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VII.  Another room in the castle.|9|1281
summary: King Claudius tells Laertes that, during a fencing wager, he will offer Hamlet a poisoned drink if the poisoned sword fails. Queen Gertrude enters and tells Laertes that his sister Ophelia has drowned. When Laertes asks where, Gertrude describes how a willow branch broke as Ophelia hung garlands on it, and how Ophelia floated in the brook, singing and seemingly unaware of her danger.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE VII.  Another room in the castle.|10|1441
summary: Gertrude says Ophelia’s clothes briefly kept her afloat while she sang, but then became waterlogged and pulled her down to her death. Laertes weeps despite trying to hold back his tears, saying that grief has stifled his anger. Claudius fears the news will rekindle Laertes’s rage and asks Gertrude to follow him.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|1|1
summary: Two gravediggers discuss whether Ophelia deserves a Christian burial after drowning, and the second says the coroner has approved it. The first jokes that she must have drowned in self-defense, then argues that someone who goes into the water is responsible for their death. The second suggests she would not receive a Christian burial if she were not a gentlewoman.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|2|161
summary: Two gravediggers discuss whether a woman who drowned herself should receive a Christian burial. They agree that her high social rank has given her an unfair privilege, and the first gravedigger cites the coroner’s decision as law. He then jokes that Adam was a gentleman because he had arms, and asks a riddle about who builds the strongest structures; the second suggests the gallows-maker.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|4|481
summary: Hamlet wonders how the gravedigger can sing while digging a grave, and Horatio says habit has made the work easy for him. Watching the man toss a skull, Hamlet imagines it belonged to a scheming politician or a flattering courtier and reflects bitterly that a once-living person is now food for worms and treated like a plaything; Horatio agrees that his guesses are possible.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|3|321
summary: The first gravedigger teases the second about a riddle, explaining that a gravedigger builds the strongest houses because graves last until doomsday, then sends him for liquor. As the first gravedigger digs and sings, Hamlet wonders at his lack of feeling; Horatio says familiarity makes the work easy, and Hamlet agrees that those who work less are more sensitive.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|5|641
summary: Hamlet watches a gravedigger sing as he handles bones with a shovel, and he is disturbed that a person’s remains can be treated so roughly. Seeing another skull, Hamlet imagines it belonged to a lawyer and wonders what became of his legal tricks and land purchases when all he has left is a skull full of dirt.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|6|801
summary: Hamlet reflects that a landowner’s legal documents cannot give him more space in death than his grave, and mocks people who rely on parchment for security. Horatio agrees and explains what parchment is made from. Hamlet then trades jokes with a gravedigger about whose grave he is digging, but the man says it is for neither a man nor a woman.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|7|961
summary: Hamlet questions a gravedigger about whom he is burying, but the man answers with wordplay, prompting Hamlet to complain to Horatio that people must speak precisely to avoid being misled. The gravedigger says he began work on the day Hamlet was born and that the prince was sent to England because he was mad, adding that he might recover there.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|9|1281
summary: The gravedigger tells Hamlet that a skull buried for twenty-three years belonged to Yorick, the king’s jester, who once poured wine on his head. Hamlet takes the skull and recalls Yorick’s wit, affection, and laughter, but feels sick at the sight of his remains. He says that even a heavily made-up lady must eventually look like this.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|8|1121
summary: Hamlet questions the gravedigger, who says Hamlet was sent to England because he was mad and jokes that his madness would go unnoticed among the equally mad English. The gravedigger says he has worked there for thirty years, explains how long bodies take to decay, and shows Hamlet a skull that has been buried for twenty-three years.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|10|1441
summary: Hamlet mocks a skull’s silent grin and says that even a heavily made-up lady will eventually look like it. He tells Horatio that Alexander’s remains could become clay used to plug a beer barrel, and Caesar’s could patch a wall; Horatio thinks this speculation goes too far. Hamlet then tells Horatio to step aside because the king is coming.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|11|1601
summary: Hamlet reflects that the remains of a once powerful person might become clay used to block the wind. Seeing the king, queen and mourners at Ophelia’s funeral, he hides and suspects that the limited rites mean she killed herself. Laertes asks for more ceremony, but the priest says her death was doubtful and that she has already been granted exceptional honors.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|13|1921
summary: Laertes calls for earth to be piled into a mountain, and Hamlet steps forward, questioning his extravagant grief and identifying himself. Laertes curses Hamlet and grabs his throat, but others try to separate and calm them. Hamlet declares that he loved Ophelia more than thousands of brothers could and challenges Laertes to show what he would do for her.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|2|161
summary: Hamlet tells Horatio that a royal order called for his immediate execution, and Horatio is shocked. Hamlet explains that he wrote a replacement order asking the English king to execute its bearers immediately, without giving them time to confess their sins; he is grateful that his skill at writing neatly helped him. Horatio asks how he sealed the document.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|12|1761
summary: The priest says Ophelia can have only limited funeral rites, angering Laertes, who says his sister will become an angel. Hamlet realizes that Ophelia has died, and Gertrude scatters flowers, mourning the marriage she had hoped Ophelia would have with him. Laertes curses whoever destroyed her mind and leaps into her grave to hold her; Hamlet steps forward and questions this extravagant display of grief.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|14|2081
summary: Hamlet challenges Laertes, saying he will match any show of grief for Ophelia, even being buried alive with her, and asks why Laertes treats him badly when he has always loved him. Gertrude calls Hamlet’s behavior madness that will soon pass, while Claudius asks Horatio to attend him, tells Laertes to be patient until they act on their plan, and asks Gertrude to watch her son.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|4|481
summary: Hamlet tells Horatio that Claudius killed his father, slept with his mother, took the throne he hoped to inherit, and plotted to kill him. He argues that killing Claudius would be justified, then regrets losing his temper with Laertes and resolves to seek his favor. When Osric arrives, Hamlet mocks him as a foolish but wealthy landowner.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|1|1
summary: Hamlet tells Horatio that restless fear drove him from his ship’s cabin to find and open a sealed commission. He discovered that it ordered his immediate execution, supposedly for the safety of Denmark and England, and says that rash actions can succeed when careful plans fail because a divine power shapes outcomes. Horatio agrees and is shocked by the order.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  A churchyard.|15|2241
summary: King Claudius tells Horatio to attend Hamlet, and Horatio leaves. Claudius urges Laertes to remain patient and says they will soon act on what they discussed the previous night; he asks Gertrude to keep watch over Hamlet and promises a living monument for the grave and a peaceful hour soon.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|5|641
summary: Hamlet mocks Osric as a foolish man whose only distinction is his wealth and land. Osric says he has a message from the king, while Hamlet tells him to put on his hat and teases him by changing his mind about the temperature. Osric says the king has made a large wager on Hamlet and begins praising Laertes.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|3|321
summary: Hamlet tells Horatio that he forged a sealed order for Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to be killed immediately, using his father’s signet to make the substitution undetectable. He feels no guilt because they willingly took the assignment. Horatio condemns the king, and Hamlet asks whether he is justified in killing him, accusing him of murdering his father, seducing his mother, blocking his succession, and plotting his death.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|9|1281
summary: Hamlet tells Osric that he is ready to fence in the hall and will try to win for the king, though he risks embarrassment if he loses. After Osric leaves, Hamlet and Horatio mock him, and Hamlet criticizes fashionable courtiers for having polished manners but little substance. A lord then begins to report the king’s response.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|6|801
summary: Osric tells Hamlet that Laertes has just arrived at court and praises him as an exceptionally refined gentleman. Hamlet responds with elaborate, exaggerated praise, then asks why Osric has brought Laertes up. Horatio mocks Osric’s flowery language, saying he has already run out of fine words.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|7|961
summary: Hamlet asks why Osric has mentioned Laertes, while he and Horatio mock Osric’s elaborate language. Osric praises Laertes’s skill with rapier and dagger and explains that the king has wagered six horses against Laertes’s six French rapiers and daggers, with their accessories; Hamlet asks what Osric means by “carriages.”

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|11|1601
summary: Hamlet admits to Horatio that he has an uneasy feeling, but rejects Horatio’s offer to excuse him, saying that what matters is being ready for whatever happens. King Claudius tells Hamlet to take Laertes’ hand, and Hamlet asks Laertes to forgive him, blaming his wrongdoing on madness rather than his true self.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|8|1121
summary: Osric describes a wager involving six horses, six swords, and their accessories, while Hamlet and Horatio mock his elaborate language. Osric explains that the king has bet that Laertes will not outscore Hamlet by more than three hits in twelve passes. Hamlet says he is ready to fence if Laertes agrees and the king still wants the match.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|10|1441
summary: A lord asks whether Hamlet is still willing to fence Laertes and says the king and queen are coming. Hamlet agrees and accepts the queen’s advice to treat Laertes gently. Horatio predicts Hamlet will lose, but Hamlet trusts his practice and the odds, despite a troubling feeling in his heart; Horatio urges him to heed it.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|12|1761
summary: Hamlet tells Laertes that madness, not his true self, caused the harm he did, and asks Laertes to regard it as an unintended injury. Laertes accepts his friendship but says he cannot formally reconcile until respected authorities assure him his honor is safe. Hamlet agrees to fence with him, joking that Laertes’s skill will shine against his own inexperience.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|16|2401
summary: Hamlet orders the door locked, and Laertes reveals that the sword is poisoned, both men are dying, Hamlet’s mother has been poisoned, and King Claudius is responsible. Hamlet attacks the king and makes him drink poison; Laertes says the king deserves it and asks Hamlet to exchange forgiveness, which Hamlet grants before telling Horatio that he is dying.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|14|2081
summary: King Claudius orders a pearl placed in a cup and toasts Hamlet as Hamlet and Laertes fence; Osric confirms Hamlet’s first hit, and Laertes admits a second. Queen Gertrude offers to wipe Hamlet’s face and drinks to his success despite Claudius’s warning. Claudius privately reveals that the cup is poisoned, while Laertes says he will hit Hamlet now.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|13|1921
summary: Hamlet gladly agrees to fence with Laertes and says that Laertes’s skill will make his own look poor, though Laertes suspects he is mocking him. As they choose their swords, King Claudius explains that he has bet on Hamlet with favorable odds and orders wine and a cannon salute if Hamlet scores an early hit.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|15|2241
summary: Queen Gertrude offers to wipe Hamlet’s face, while King Claudius privately reveals that her drink is poisoned. Hamlet urges Laertes to fight harder; both are wounded, and Laertes admits that his own treachery has fatally trapped him. Gertrude says she has been poisoned, prompting Hamlet to order the doors locked and the betrayal investigated; Laertes tells him he too is dying.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|17|2561
