summary: Dying from poison, Hamlet asks Horatio to stay alive and tell his story truthfully, fearing that his reputation will suffer if the facts remain unknown. Horatio wants to drink from the cup, but Hamlet stops him. Osric explains that the distant noise comes from Fortinbras, who has returned victorious from Poland, and Hamlet gives Fortinbras his dying vote for the throne.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|18|2721
summary: As Hamlet dies, he predicts that Fortinbras will be elected king, gives him his support, and asks Horatio to tell him what happened. Horatio mourns Hamlet, and Fortinbras is horrified by the bloody scene. An English ambassador reports that Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are dead, but Horatio says the dead king never ordered their deaths.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|19|2881
summary: Horatio asks that the bodies be displayed and offers to explain the bloody deaths, including accidents, plots, and plans that backfired. Fortinbras is eager to hear him and, though sorrowful, intends to claim his rights in Denmark. Horatio urges them to act quickly to prevent further trouble, and Fortinbras orders four captains to carry Hamlet to the stage like a soldier.

key: hamlet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  A hall in the castle.|20|3041
summary: Horatio urges immediate action while people are still upset, fearing that more trouble may arise from plots and mistakes. Fortinbras orders four captains to carry Hamlet to a raised platform with military music and honors, saying he would likely have been an excellent king; he also orders the bodies removed and the soldiers to fire their weapons.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A camp near Forres.|1|1
summary: King Duncan asks about a wounded man, and Malcolm identifies him as a brave sergeant who fought to prevent his capture. The sergeant reports that the battle was evenly matched until Macbeth fought his way to the rebel Macdonwald, killed him, and displayed his head on the battlements; Duncan praises Macbeth, but the sergeant warns that trouble followed this success.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A camp near Forres.|2|161
summary: The wounded sergeant reports that a defeated enemy’s head was placed on the battlements and that Macbeth and Banquo fought fiercely when Norwegian forces launched a fresh attack. Duncan praises their courage and orders surgeons to treat the sergeant. Malcolm identifies the hurried newcomer as Ross, who tells Duncan he has come from Fife.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  A desert place.|1|1
summary: Three witches arrange to meet Macbeth on the heath before sunset, after the battle is over. Responding to calls from Graymalkin and Paddock, they prepare to leave, declaring that what is fair is foul and what is foul is fair, as they move through the fog and dirty air.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A camp near Forres.|3|321
summary: Ross tells King Duncan that Macbeth defeated the Norwegian king and the traitorous thane of Cawdor, and that Norway must pay ten thousand dollars before burying its dead. Delighted by the victory, Duncan orders Cawdor’s execution and gives his title to Macbeth; Ross promises to carry out the orders.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A heath near Forres.|2|161
summary: The three witches announce Macbeth’s approach and perform a charm. Macbeth remarks on the strange weather, while Banquo is puzzled by the witches’ wild appearance and beards. When Macbeth asks who they are, they hail him as thane of Glamis and Cawdor and predict that he will be king; Banquo wonders why Macbeth seems frightened by their welcome.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A heath near Forres.|4|481
summary: Macbeth demands to know how the witches learned their strange prophecies, but they vanish, leaving him wishing they had stayed and Banquo wondering whether they imagined the encounter. They recall the predictions that Macbeth will be king and thane of Cawdor, and that Banquo’s children will be kings. Ross arrives and tells Macbeth that the king is delighted by reports of his courage against the rebels and Norwegians.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A heath near Forres.|5|641
summary: Ross praises Macbeth’s fearless fighting against the Norwegians and, with Angus, brings the king’s thanks and summons. Ross names Macbeth thane of Cawdor, prompting Banquo to wonder whether the devil can tell the truth; Macbeth protests that the current thane still lives. Angus explains that the man is condemned for treason, while Macbeth privately reflects that a greater honor is still to come.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A heath near Forres.|3|321
summary: Banquo asks why Macbeth seems afraid of the witches’ promising predictions, questions whether the witches are real, and asks them to foretell his future. The witches say he will be both lesser and greater than Macbeth and father kings without becoming one himself. Macbeth demands to know how they learned their predictions, doubting that he could become Thane of Cawdor or king.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A heath near Forres.|1|1
summary: The three witches discuss their activities: one has killed pigs, and another plans to torment a sailor because his wife refused to share her chestnuts. With winds from her sisters, she will make him sleepless and miserable and batter his ship, though she cannot sink it; she also displays a shipwrecked pilot’s thumb. Hearing a drum announce Macbeth’s arrival, the witches join hands and circle together.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A heath near Forres.|6|801
summary: Angus says the former thane of Cawdor has fallen because of proven treason. Macbeth, now thane of Cawdor, asks Banquo whether he hopes his children will be kings, as the same prophets promised. Banquo warns that dark forces may tell small truths to cause great harm, while Macbeth privately wonders whether the prophecy is good or evil and is frightened by his own thoughts.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A heath near Forres.|7|961
summary: Macbeth is horrified by thoughts of murder and considers letting chance make him king without acting. Banquo notices that Macbeth is distracted and says his new honors will take time to get used to. Macbeth apologizes, thanks the gentlemen, and suggests they go to the king and later speak openly about what has happened; Banquo agrees.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  Forres. The palace.|2|161
summary: Duncan tells Macbeth that he deserves more than anyone can repay, while Macbeth says that loyal service is its own reward. Duncan warmly embraces Banquo, expresses tears of joy, names his eldest son Malcolm Prince of Cumberland, and promises to honor others who deserve it. He announces that he will go to Inverness, and Macbeth says that any work not done for Duncan is a burden.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  Forres. The palace.|1|1
summary: Duncan asks about Cawdor’s execution, and Malcolm reports that he confessed his treason, begged for pardon, and died calmly and repentantly. Duncan laments that he trusted Cawdor and could not read his thoughts from his face, then tells Macbeth that no reward can match his service; Macbeth replies that serving loyally is its own reward.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Inverness. Macbeth's castle.|1|1
summary: Lady Macbeth reads a letter in which Macbeth describes meeting the witches, who vanished after predicting he would become Thane of Cawdor and then king; he soon received word that he was Thane of Cawdor. Lady Macbeth believes he will become king, but fears he is too kind and unwilling to do wrong to gain power quickly.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Inverness. Macbeth's castle.|3|321
summary: Lady Macbeth tells a messenger to be cared for, then calls on evil spirits to fill her with cruelty and block any remorse as she plans Duncan’s death. When Macbeth arrives and says Duncan will visit that night and intends to leave tomorrow, she declares that he will never see tomorrow and says Macbeth’s face reveals his thoughts.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  Forres. The palace.|3|321
summary: Duncan promises honors to all who deserve them and says he will visit Macbeth at Inverness; Macbeth offers to go ahead and tell his wife. Privately, Macbeth sees the Prince of Cumberland as an obstacle and wishes to hide his dark desires. Duncan praises Macbeth to Banquo and proposes following him.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Inverness. Macbeth's castle.|4|481
summary: Macbeth tells Lady Macbeth that King Duncan is coming to their castle tonight and plans to leave tomorrow. Lady Macbeth declares that Duncan will not live to see tomorrow and tells Macbeth to hide his intentions behind a welcoming appearance. Macbeth wants to discuss the matter further, but she tells him to leave the arrangements to her.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  Inverness. Macbeth's castle.|2|161
summary: Lady Macbeth says that Macbeth wants power but lacks the ruthlessness to seize it, and she hopes to persuade him to take the crown. A messenger tells her that King Duncan will arrive that night; after initially doubting him, she calls the news great and summons spirits associated with deadly thoughts to strip her of her womanhood.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE VI.  Before Macbeth's castle.|1|1
summary: Outside Macbeth’s castle, Duncan praises its pleasant setting and fresh air, and Banquo points to the many nesting birds as a sign of the air’s sweetness. Lady Macbeth says that no amount of service could repay the honors Duncan has given her family. Duncan thanks her for her trouble and asks where Macbeth is, noting that he rode home ahead of them.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE VI.  Before Macbeth's castle.|2|161
summary: King Duncan tells Lady Macbeth that he had hoped to arrive before Macbeth and prepare for him, but Macbeth rode quickly home out of love. Lady Macbeth assures Duncan that she and her household are at his service, and Duncan asks her to lead him to Macbeth, whom he loves and intends to continue favoring.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE VII.  Macbeth's castle.|1|1
summary: Macbeth considers killing King Duncan and wishes the murder could be done quickly without consequences, but fears that violence will return to punish him. He recognizes that Duncan trusts him as a relative, subject, and host, and believes the king’s goodness would make his murder a cause of widespread grief.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE VII.  Macbeth's castle.|2|161
summary: Macbeth imagines that killing Duncan would cause overwhelming grief and admits that ambition is his only motive. When Lady Macbeth says Duncan has nearly finished eating and has asked for him, Macbeth decides not to go ahead, wanting to preserve his honors and good reputation. Lady Macbeth mocks his change of heart, questions his love, and accuses him of fearing to act on his desires.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE VII.  Macbeth's castle.|3|321
summary: Lady Macbeth accuses Macbeth of cowardice for shrinking from the plan he proposed, even though the time and place are now favorable. She says she would kill her own nursing baby rather than break such a promise. Macbeth insists that a man should not go beyond what is honorable and asks what will happen if they fail; she urges him to be brave and assures him they will succeed.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE VII.  Macbeth's castle.|4|481
summary: Lady Macbeth says she would have killed her nursing baby if she had sworn to do so, and urges Macbeth to be brave when he fears failure. She plans to get Duncan’s guards drunk so they can kill the sleeping king and blame the guards; Macbeth admires her courage, agrees, and resolves to hide their intentions behind a pleasant appearance.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE VII.  Macbeth's castle.|5|641
summary: Lady Macbeth says that their loud expressions of grief over the death will make others believe their account. Macbeth declares that he is resolved to carry out the terrible act, and he urges them to present a pleasant appearance that hides their deceitful intentions.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  Court of Macbeth's castle.|1|1
summary: Banquo tells his son Fleance that he is tired but fears troubling thoughts in sleep. When Macbeth arrives, Banquo says the king has gone to bed happy and has sent Lady Macbeth a diamond. Banquo mentions dreaming of the three witches and says some of their predictions have come true; Macbeth claims not to think of them but suggests they talk later.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  Court of Macbeth's castle.|2|161
summary: Banquo says the predictions have proved partly true. Macbeth proposes discussing them later and promises Banquo honor for his support, but Banquo agrees only if he can remain loyal and honorable. After telling a servant to have Lady Macbeth ring a bell when his drink is ready, Macbeth sees a dagger he cannot grasp and wonders if it is imaginary.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  Court of Macbeth's castle.|3|321
summary: Macbeth sees a dagger leading him toward the murder he plans, then notices blood on it and decides that his troubled mind has created the vision. He describes the dark night as a time of nightmares and stealthy violence, and begs the earth not to reveal his footsteps. When a bell rings, he takes it as his signal to go and kill Duncan.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  Court of Macbeth's castle.|4|481
summary: Macbeth says that Duncan remains alive while he talks, and that words weaken his resolve to act. When a bell rings, Macbeth takes it as a signal to go and kill Duncan, hoping Duncan does not hear the bell that calls him to heaven or hell.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  The same.|1|1
summary: Lady Macbeth says she has drugged the guards and left their daggers ready, but could not kill King Duncan herself because he looked like her father. Macbeth returns and says he has killed him; disturbed by the sight of his hands, he describes hearing sleeping men wake, cry out, and pray.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  The same.|2|161
summary: Macbeth is troubled by his bloody hands and tells Lady Macbeth that two sleeping men woke, prayed, and went back to sleep, while he could not say “Amen” despite needing a blessing. He says he heard a voice declare that he has murdered sleep and will sleep no more; Lady Macbeth urges him not to dwell on what they have done, fearing it will drive them mad.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  The same.|3|321
summary: Macbeth says a voice cried that he has murdered sleep and will never sleep again. Lady Macbeth tells him to wash his bloody hands and return the daggers, but he is too afraid, so she takes them and plans to smear the sleeping guards with blood to make them look guilty. Startled by knocking, Macbeth feels that even the ocean cannot wash the blood from his hands.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  The same.|4|481
summary: Macbeth is terrified by the knocking and believes that all the water in the ocean could not wash the blood from his hands. Lady Macbeth says her hands are equally bloody but scolds him for his fear, urging him to wash, put on his nightgown, and return to their chamber. Macbeth wishes the knocking could wake Duncan.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  The same.|2|161
summary: The porter hears knocking and asks to be remembered for letting the visitors in. When Macduff asks why he is up so late, the porter says he was drinking and jokes that alcohol causes a red nose, sleep and urination, while raising sexual desire but preventing performance. Macduff asks whether the porter’s master is awake, and Macbeth enters.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  The same.|1|1
summary: The porter, annoyed by persistent knocking, jokes that he is guarding the gates of hell and imagines admitting a farmer who hanged himself, a deceitful traitor, and a thieving tailor. He gives up the joke and answers the door; Macduff asks why he is up so late, and the porter begins to explain that they were drinking.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  The same.|5|641
summary: Lady Macbeth asks why an alarm has awakened the household, and Macduff tells Banquo that King Duncan has been murdered. Banquo begs him to deny it, while Macbeth declares that life has lost its value. Macduff tells Malcolm and Donalbain their father is dead, and Lennox says the king’s attendants appeared responsible, with blood on their hands, faces, and daggers.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  The same.|4|481
summary: Lennox describes an owl crying all night and reports that some people say the earth shook; Macbeth agrees that the night was rough. A horrified Macduff announces that the king has been murdered, sends Macbeth and Lennox to see, and calls for an alarm to wake the household. When Lady Macbeth asks what has happened, Macduff says the news is too terrible for her to hear.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  The same.|3|321
summary: The Porter jokes about overcoming an opponent despite being knocked off his feet. Macduff asks after the king, whom he is supposed to wake, and Macbeth leads him to the door. Lennox describes a terrifying night of high winds, strange cries, ominous prophecies, and an earthquake; Macbeth agrees it was rough, and Macduff cries out in horror.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  The same.|6|801
summary: Lennox tells Malcolm that Duncan’s attendants appeared to be the killers, with blood on their faces, hands, and daggers. Macbeth regrets killing them, saying his love for Duncan drove him into a fury; Lady Macbeth calls for help, and Macduff asks others to attend to her. Malcolm privately questions their silence, but Donalbain warns of hidden danger and urges him to leave.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  The same.|8|1121
summary: Donalbain decides to go to Ireland, believing that he and Malcolm will be safer apart and that even smiling people, especially close relatives, may be dangerous. Malcolm agrees that the threat is not over and urges them to ride away without saying goodbye, since leaving secretly is justified when no mercy can be expected.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  Outside Macbeth's castle.|1|1
summary: An old man says the night’s horrors are worse than anything he has seen in seventy years, and Ross describes unnatural darkness during the day. They discuss an owl killing a falcon and Duncan’s horses breaking loose and eating one another. Macduff says the men Macbeth killed committed the bloody deed, and Ross asks what they hoped to gain.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  The same.|7|961
summary: Malcolm and Donalbain fear hidden danger and cannot yet show their grief. As Lady Macbeth is carried out, Banquo proposes that everyone dress and investigate the bloody crime, pledging to fight treason; Macbeth and the others agree to meet. Malcolm decides to flee to England and Donalbain to Ireland, believing they will be safer apart and that even smiling relatives may be dangerous.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  Outside Macbeth's castle.|2|161
summary: Macduff tells Ross that the men Macbeth killed are suspected of Duncan’s murder, and that Duncan’s fleeing sons are suspected of hiring them. Macbeth has been named king and gone to Scone for his coronation, while Duncan’s body has been taken to Colmekill for burial. Ross plans to attend the coronation, but Macduff goes to Fife, worried about the new reign; an old man blesses them.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  Forres. The palace.|2|161
summary: Banquo tells Macbeth that he and Fleance are going riding and promises to return for the feast, though he may be out after dark. Macbeth says their cousins are in England and Ireland, denying their father’s murder and spreading false stories, and proposes discussing this tomorrow. After Banquo and the others leave, Macbeth asks an attendant to bring in the men waiting outside the palace.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  Forres. The palace.|1|1
summary: Banquo reflects that Macbeth has gained the titles the witches promised, suspects him of foul play, and hopes their prediction that Banquo will father kings will also come true. Macbeth and Lady Macbeth welcome Banquo as an honored guest at their supper; Banquo accepts and says he will be riding until then, so Macbeth postpones seeking his advice until tomorrow.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  Forres. The palace.|3|321
summary: Macbeth dismisses his companions until supper and orders an attendant to bring in men waiting outside. Alone, he says he fears Banquo’s courage and wisdom and resents the witches’ prediction that Banquo’s descendants, rather than his own, will be kings. He feels he has corrupted himself and murdered Duncan for Banquo’s children.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  Forres. The palace.|4|481
summary: Macbeth fears that his crown will pass to someone outside his family and that he has murdered Duncan and damned his soul only to make Banquo’s descendants kings. He challenges fate, then speaks to two murderers, reminding them that he blamed Banquo for their past misfortunes instead of himself; the first murderer agrees that Macbeth made this case.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  Forres. The palace.|6|801
summary: Macbeth challenges two men to prove their manhood by killing Banquo, whom he calls their enemy and his own. The men say hardship has made them reckless and desperate enough to risk anything. Macbeth says Banquo’s life threatens his own, but he cannot openly kill him because they share friends whose loyalty he wants to keep.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  Forres. The palace.|5|641
summary: Macbeth reminds the first murderer that he has blamed Banquo for deceiving and ruining him and his companions, then asks whether they can forgive Banquo and pray for him and his children. When the murderer insists that they are men, Macbeth compares men to different breeds of dogs and challenges them to prove they are not among the lowest.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  Forres. The palace.|7|961
summary: Macbeth tells two murderers that he wants Banquo killed secretly because they share friends, and he would have to mourn Banquo’s death. He orders them to kill Banquo and his son Fleance away from the palace that night, promising to give them the exact time and place. The murderers agree and leave, while Macbeth reflects on Banquo’s death.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  Forres. The palace.|8|1121
summary: Macbeth tells the two murderers to prepare themselves for the dark task ahead and wait inside until he calls for them. They assure him that they are resolved, and after they leave, Macbeth declares that Banquo must die that night.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  The palace.|1|1
summary: A servant tells Lady Macbeth that Banquo has left court but will return that night, and she asks to speak with the king. She admits that getting what they wanted has brought no happiness and urges Macbeth to stop dwelling on the past. Macbeth says they are still in danger and tormented by fear and nightmares, while the dead Duncan rests peacefully.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The same. Hall in the palace.|1|1
summary: Macbeth welcomes the lords to a feast, and Lady Macbeth says they are welcome from her heart. A murderer tells Macbeth that he has cut Banquo’s throat, but Fleance has escaped. Macbeth praises the murderer, yet feels trapped by doubts and fears because Fleance is still alive.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  The palace.|3|321
summary: Macbeth tells Lady Macbeth that a dreadful deed will be done before night, but refuses to tell her what it is until she can applaud it. He calls on darkness to hide the act and end what makes him fearful, then tells his puzzled wife that evil deeds are strengthened by further evil and asks her to come with him.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The same. Hall in the palace.|2|161
summary: Macbeth tells the murderer that he is trapped by doubts and fears; the murderer confirms that Banquo is dead, while Macbeth says Banquo’s escaped son may become dangerous. Lady Macbeth urges her husband to welcome their guests, and he wishes them a healthy appetite. Macbeth remarks on Banquo’s absence, then says the table is full when the guests ask him to sit.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  A park near the palace.|1|1
summary: Three murderers wait for Banquo near the palace, and the third says Macbeth sent him to join them. They attack Banquo, who cries out at the betrayal and urges his son Fleance to escape and take revenge. The murderers realize they have killed Banquo but let Fleance escape, and decide to report what they have done.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  The palace.|2|161
summary: Macbeth says Duncan is at peace in death, beyond the reach of harm, while he himself is mentally tormented. Lady Macbeth urges him to look cheerful for their guests, and he asks her to flatter Banquo while hiding their true feelings. Distressed that Banquo and Fleance are alive, Macbeth takes comfort that they can be harmed and promises a terrible deed before nightfall, but keeps his wife uninformed.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The same. Hall in the palace.|3|321
summary: Macbeth regrets Banquo’s absence, but when Lennox points out his reserved seat, Macbeth sees Banquo’s bloody ghost and demands to know who is responsible. Ross says Macbeth is unwell, while Lady Macbeth urges the guests to ignore his fit; privately, she challenges his courage and dismisses the vision as fear, like the dagger he said led him to Duncan.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The same. Hall in the palace.|4|481
summary: Lady Macbeth scolds Macbeth for staring fearfully at what she says is only a stool, comparing his vision to the imaginary dagger he once described. Macbeth insists he has seen a dead man and is horrified that the murdered can rise again and drive people from their seats; Lady Macbeth reminds him that their guests need his attention.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  A Heath.|2|161
summary: Hecate says she will catch a falling drop of vapor and use magic to create spirits whose illusions will lead Macbeth to ruin, making him overconfident and contemptuous of fate and death. Hearing a song, she says her spirit is waiting for her in a cloud, and the First Witch urges the others to hurry because Hecate will soon return.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The same. Hall in the palace.|8|1121
summary: Macbeth says he is so deeply involved in bloodshed that turning back would be as hard as continuing, and that he has strange plans he must act on before examining them. Lady Macbeth says he needs sleep, and he agrees, blaming his strange fears on inexperience and saying they are still new to such deeds.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The same. Hall in the palace.|5|641
summary: Macbeth says it is strange for murdered people to rise and drive the living from their seats. Lady Macbeth reminds him of their guests, and he calls his behavior an illness before toasting them and the absent Banquo. Macbeth then orders Banquo’s ghost away, saying he would rather face a wild beast, while Lady Macbeth reassures the lords.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  A Heath.|1|1
summary: The First Witch notices that Hecate looks angry. Hecate scolds the witches for dealing with Macbeth without her and says he cares only about his own interests. She orders them to meet her at the pit of Acheron with their spells, while she prepares to create spirits whose illusions will lead Macbeth to ruin.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE VI.  Forres. The palace.|1|1
summary: Lennox speaks sarcastically about the deaths of Duncan and Banquo, casting doubt on the accusations against Duncan’s sons and Banquo’s son Fleance. He suggests that Macbeth killed Duncan’s guards to silence them and fears what Macbeth would do to the sons and Fleance if he caught them. Lennox says Macduff is reportedly out of favor and asks a lord where he is.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The same. Hall in the palace.|7|961
summary: Lady Macbeth dismisses the guests because their questions upset Macbeth, and Lennox wishes the king better health. Macbeth says murder will be exposed and asks about Macduff’s absence, revealing that he pays servants to spy on the nobles. He plans to visit the witches and learn the worst, saying he is too deep in bloodshed to turn back.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE VI.  Forres. The palace.|2|161
summary: Lennox asks where Macduff has gone, having heard that he is disgraced for missing King Macbeth’s feast. A lord says Macduff has gone to England to seek King Edward’s help and soldiers for Malcolm, hoping to restore peace and security in Scotland. He adds that Macbeth is preparing for war and that Macduff has refused his summons.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  The same. Hall in the palace.|6|801
summary: Macbeth challenges Banquo’s ghost to take another frightening shape or return alive to fight, then feels brave again when it vanishes. Lady Macbeth says his behavior has ruined the gathering, while Macbeth wonders how the others can remain calm. After Ross asks what he sees, Lady Macbeth dismisses the guests, and Macbeth says blood will have blood.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  A cavern. In the middle, a boiling cauldron.|1|1
summary: Three witches announce that animal cries signal the time, then circle a boiling cauldron and add a toad, animal parts, poisonous plants, and human remains to make a powerful, harmful charm. As they work, they repeatedly chant for the fire to burn and the cauldron to bubble.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  A cavern. In the middle, a boiling cauldron.|5|641
summary: Macbeth anxiously asks the witches whether Banquo’s descendants will rule Scotland, and threatens to curse them when they warn him to ask no more. The witches show him a long line of crowned figures, the last holding a mirror that reveals many more; Macbeth is horrified to see Banquo’s bloodstained spirit smiling and pointing to them as his descendants.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  A cavern. In the middle, a boiling cauldron.|4|481
summary: An apparition tells Macbeth to be bold because no one born of a woman can harm him, but Macbeth decides to have Macduff killed anyway to ease his fears. A crowned child then says Macbeth cannot be defeated until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane Hill; Macbeth believes this is impossible and feels reassured, but still wants to know about Banquo’s descendants.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  A cavern. In the middle, a boiling cauldron.|2|161
summary: The witches add gruesome ingredients to their boiling cauldron and chant, while Hecate praises them, promises them a share of the rewards, and tells them to sing around it. The second witch senses something wicked approaching, and Macbeth arrives and demands answers, even if their magic brings destruction upon the world. The first witch tells him to speak.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  A cavern. In the middle, a boiling cauldron.|3|321
summary: Macbeth demands answers from the witches, even if nature and great buildings are destroyed, and asks to see their masters. After the witches add ingredients to the fire and summon spirits, one warns Macbeth to beware of Macduff, confirming his fear. Another tells him to be bold because no one born of a woman can harm him, but Macbeth still wants extra assurance against Macduff.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE VI.  Forres. The palace.|3|321
summary: The Lord describes a gloomy messenger turning away and muttering after a blunt refusal, as if warning that the refusal will be regretted. Lennox says the warning might encourage caution and distance; he hopes an angel will carry the message quickly to England and bring relief to Scotland, which suffers under a cursed ruler. The Lord adds his prayers.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  A cavern. In the middle, a boiling cauldron.|6|801
summary: Macbeth is horrified by a vision of Banquo pointing out a line of kings as his descendants, and the first witch confirms that the vision is true. The witches try to cheer Macbeth before vanishing, and he curses them and the hour. Lennox tells Macbeth that Macduff has fled to England, prompting Macbeth to reflect that he must act on his plans quickly.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE II.  Fife. Macduff's castle.|1|1
summary: Lady Macduff angrily asks why her husband fled Scotland, leaving her and their children behind, and says his fear shows a lack of love and courage. Ross urges her to be patient, defends Macduff as wise and noble, and describes the times as cruel and frightening before taking his leave.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  A cavern. In the middle, a boiling cauldron.|7|961
summary: Lennox tells Macbeth that messengers have brought word that Macduff has fled to England. Macbeth decides to act immediately on his intentions: he will attack Macduff’s castle, seize Fife, and kill Macduff’s wife, children, and descendants; he then asks Lennox to take him to the messengers.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE II.  Fife. Macduff's castle.|2|161
summary: Ross describes the uncertainty and fear surrounding them, hopes things will improve, and leaves Lady Macduff and her son before he becomes too emotional. Lady Macduff says her son is fatherless and tells him his father is dead, but the boy refuses to believe her; they joke about how he would live and how she would find another husband.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE II.  Fife. Macduff's castle.|3|321
summary: Lady Macduff tells her son that his father is dead and was a traitor, while they joke about finding new spouses and parents. When she says traitors lie and must be hanged by honest men, her son argues that liars are numerous enough to hang the honest men instead. A messenger arrives, blesses Lady Macduff, and says he knows her high rank, though she does not know him.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|1|1
summary: Malcolm suggests they find a lonely place to mourn, but Macduff urges him to fight for Scotland, where new suffering arises every day. Malcolm promises to address what he can, but suspects Macduff might betray him to Macbeth, whom Macduff once loved. Macduff denies being a traitor, and Malcolm acknowledges that appearances cannot prove a person’s true nature.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE II.  Fife. Macduff's castle.|4|481
summary: Lady Macduff’s son jokes about getting a new father before a messenger warns her to flee with her children. She wonders where to go and reflects that innocence offers little protection in a world that rewards wrongdoing. A murderer asks for her husband and calls him a traitor; when her son protests, the murderer stabs him, and the boy urges his mother to run.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|3|321
summary: Malcolm says Scotland suffers under Macbeth and that England has offered him thousands of soldiers, but he claims that he would make the country suffer even more if he became king. Macduff insists that no devil could be worse than Macbeth, but Malcolm says his own lust for women is limitless, even as he acknowledges Macbeth’s many crimes and vices.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|2|161
summary: Malcolm tells Macduff that appearances can be deceptive and questions why he left his wife and child without saying goodbye, explaining that his suspicions are meant to protect himself. Macduff loses hope and laments Scotland’s suffering under tyranny, insisting he is not the villain Malcolm suspects. Malcolm asks him not to be offended and agrees that Scotland suffers, adding that he believes people would support his claim.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|4|481
summary: Malcolm claims that his lust is so insatiable that Macbeth would be a better ruler than he would. Macduff admits that such excess has ruined kings, but urges Malcolm to claim the throne, saying he can conceal his pleasures and find willing women. Malcolm adds that his greed would drive him to invent charges against loyal nobles and kill them for their wealth.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|5|641
summary: Malcolm says he would greedily seize nobles’ wealth, invent reasons to destroy loyal people, and disrupt peace everywhere. Macduff calls greed dangerous but says Scotland could satisfy it if Malcolm had other virtues. When Malcolm claims to have no virtues at all, Macduff declares him unfit to rule or live and mourns for Scotland under its bloody tyrant.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|6|801
summary: Macduff declares Malcolm unfit to live or rule, mourns Scotland under the bloody tyrant Macbeth, praises Malcolm’s parents, and says his hope is gone. Moved by Macduff’s honest grief, Malcolm admits that fear of Macbeth’s traps made him suspicious, takes back the faults he claimed, and says he is chaste and truthful.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|7|961
summary: Malcolm takes back the faults he claimed to have, declares his honesty and loyalty, and says he and Macduff will join Siward and his ten thousand soldiers. Macduff struggles to reconcile the good and bad things he has heard. A doctor says the English king can heal people whom medicine cannot cure, and Malcolm identifies their disease as the evil.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|10|1441
summary: Ross urges Malcolm to help Scotland, saying his presence would inspire people to fight their suffering. Malcolm says he is coming with Siward and ten thousand English soldiers. Ross then reluctantly tells Macduff that his castle has been attacked and his wife and children brutally killed, leaving Malcolm shocked.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|9|1281
summary: Ross tells Macduff and Malcolm that Scotland has become a place of constant suffering and sudden death, where only the unaware can smile. When Macduff asks about his wife and children, Ross says they were well and at peace when he left. Ross reports rumors of resistance to the tyrant and urges Malcolm to come to Scotland, saying his presence would inspire people to fight.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|11|1601
summary: Ross tells Macduff that his castle was attacked and his wife, children, and servants were killed. Malcolm urges him to express his grief and seek revenge, but Macduff struggles to believe that his loved ones are dead, insists that a man must feel sorrow, and blames himself for their deaths.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  Dunsinane. Ante-room in the castle.|1|1
summary: The gentlewoman tells the doctor that Lady Macbeth has been walking and performing tasks in her sleep since Macbeth went to war, but she refuses to repeat what Lady Macbeth has said without a witness. Lady Macbeth enters carrying a candle, and the gentlewoman explains that she insists on keeping a light nearby and is asleep despite her open eyes.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|8|1121
summary: After thanking the doctor, Malcolm tells Macduff that England’s king heals people with a disease by placing a gold coin around their necks and praying, and that he can also prophesy. Ross arrives, and Malcolm wishes for an end to the conditions keeping Scots apart. Asked about Scotland, Ross mournfully describes a land of death, suffering, and cries that go unnoticed.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  England. Before the King's palace.|12|1761
summary: Macduff blames himself for the slaughter of his family and prays for their souls, while Malcolm urges him to turn his grief into anger. Macduff asks heaven to bring him face to face with Macbeth so he can fight him. Malcolm approves and says their army is ready, they need only the king’s permission, and better days will come.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  Dunsinane. Ante-room in the castle.|2|161
summary: A gentlewoman tells the doctor that Lady Macbeth keeps a light nearby and often rubs her hands as if washing them while asleep. Lady Macbeth tries to remove an imagined spot, speaks of an old man’s blood, asks where the thane of Fife’s wife is, and scolds her fearful husband; the doctor writes down her words.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  Dunsinane. Ante-room in the castle.|3|321
summary: Lady Macbeth asks whether her hands will ever be clean, says they still smell of blood, and sighs in distress. She tells her husband to wash, reminds him that Banquo is buried, and urges him to bed, saying that what is done cannot be undone. The doctor and gentlewoman are troubled by her words, and the doctor says her illness is beyond his skill.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  Dunsinane. Ante-room in the castle.|4|481
summary: Lady Macbeth speaks of knocking at the gate, asks for a hand, and insists it is time for bed, saying that what is done cannot be undone. The doctor is disturbed by her words and says she needs a priest more than a physician. He tells the gentlewoman to remove anything that could harm her and keep watch over her.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  The country near Dunsinane.|1|1
summary: Menteith says English forces led by Malcolm, Siward and Macduff are approaching, driven by revenge, and Angus says they will meet near Birnam Wood. Lennox confirms that Donalbain is absent, while Caithness reports that Macbeth is fortifying Dunsinane and may be mad. Angus and Menteith describe Macbeth as guilty, insecure and obeyed without love, and Caithness urges the others to march on.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  Dunsinane. A room in the castle.|1|1
summary: Macbeth refuses further reports of desertion, insisting he cannot fear Malcolm because the spirits have said he is safe until Birnam Wood moves to Dunsinane and no man born of a woman can harm him. He mocks a frightened servant who reports ten thousand English soldiers, then calls for Seyton and reflects sadly on aging and the coming battle, which will either secure or end his rule.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  The country near Dunsinane.|2|161
summary: Angus compares Macbeth to a thief wearing a giant’s robe, and Menteith says Macbeth’s troubled mind is shaken by guilt. Caithness urges the others to march and join the man who can heal their country, offering their lives if necessary; Lennox agrees, saying they should support their rightful ruler and destroy his enemies as they march toward Birnam.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE V.  Dunsinane. Within the castle.|2|161
summary: Macbeth reflects bitterly that time drags on and life is brief and meaningless. A messenger reports seeing Birnam Wood moving toward the castle, and Macbeth calls him a liar and threatens to hang him until he starves if the report is false. If it is true, Macbeth says he no longer cares about his own life, and he begins to doubt the fiend’s deceptive prophecy.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE V.  Dunsinane. Within the castle.|1|1
summary: Macbeth orders banners hung on the castle walls, confident that its defenses can withstand a siege, though he regrets that some of his own people have joined the enemy. Hearing women cry out, he says he has grown numb to horror. Seyton tells him that the queen is dead, and Macbeth reflects bitterly on the slow passage of time and the briefness of life.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE IV.  Country near Birnam wood.|1|1
summary: Malcolm hopes homes will soon be safe and orders each soldier to carry a branch from Birnam Wood to conceal the army’s size. Siward reports that the tyrant remains confident at Dunsinane, while Malcolm says his supporters have deserted or serve unwillingly. Macduff urges the soldiers to focus on fighting, and Siward says the battle will settle their uncertain hopes.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  Dunsinane. A room in the castle.|3|321
summary: Macbeth asks the doctor to cure a troubled mind, but the doctor says the patient must heal herself. Dismissing medicine, Macbeth orders his armor, complains that his nobles are deserting him, and asks how to drive out the English. He declares he will not fear death until Birnam forest comes to Dunsinane, while the doctor privately wishes to leave and never return.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  Dunsinane. A room in the castle.|2|161
summary: Macbeth says the coming battle will secure or end his rule, and regrets having secret curses and forced respect instead of love and honor. Seyton confirms the reports, and Macbeth vows to fight, demands his armor, and orders riders sent out and fearful talkers hanged. The doctor says his patient cannot sleep because of troubling thoughts, and Macbeth asks him to cure her mind.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE V.  Dunsinane. Within the castle.|3|321
summary: Macbeth threatens to hang and starve the messenger if his report is false, but says the messenger may do the same to him if it is true. Seeing Birnam Wood apparently advancing on Dunsinane, Macbeth doubts the fiend’s misleading promise, orders the alarm sounded, and prepares to fight, weary of life but determined to die armed.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE VI.  Dunsinane. Before the castle.|1|1
summary: Malcolm orders his soldiers to throw down their leafy screens and reveal themselves, and appoints his uncle Siward and Siward’s son to lead the first attack. Siward confidently declares that they are ready to fight the tyrant’s forces, while Macduff calls for the trumpets to sound, announcing bloodshed and death.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE VII.  Another part of the field.|1|1
summary: Macbeth says he is trapped and must fight, but fears only a man not born of a woman. Young Siward calls Macbeth a hated tyrant and threatens him with his sword, while Macbeth dismisses his weapon. Macduff searches for Macbeth, determined to kill him for his wife and children and unwilling to fight ordinary soldiers; Siward directs his companion onward.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE VIII.  Another part of the field.|3|321
summary: Ross tells Siward that his son died bravely in battle, and Siward takes comfort in learning that his wounds were in front; Malcolm says the young man deserves more grief. Macduff displays Macbeth’s severed head and declares Malcolm king of a free Scotland, and everyone joins his salute. Malcolm promises to recognize their loyalty.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE VII.  Another part of the field.|2|161
summary: Macduff says his sword remains unused and hopes that the loud fighting will lead him to Macbeth. Siward tells Malcolm that the castle has surrendered, the tyrant’s men are fighting on both sides, and victory is near. Malcolm says their enemies have missed them with their blows, and Siward urges him to enter the castle.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE VIII.  Another part of the field.|2|161
summary: Macbeth says deceptive promises have failed him and refuses to fight Macduff, but when Macduff threatens to display him as a captured tyrant, Macbeth refuses to surrender and challenges him. Malcolm hopes his missing friends are safe, while Siward accepts that some losses were inevitable; Ross reports that Siward’s son died bravely in battle, and Siward asks whether he is dead.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE VIII.  Another part of the field.|4|481
summary: Macduff and the others hail Malcolm as King of Scotland. Malcolm thanks his supporters, makes his thanes and kinsmen earls, and promises to bring exiles home and deal with the cruel agents of Macbeth and his queen, who is believed to have killed herself. He invites everyone to his coronation at Scone.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|prologue|None|1|1
summary: The Chorus describes two equally noble families in Verona whose old feud erupts into bloodshed. Their children, two doomed lovers, die and bring their parents’ hatred to an end; the Chorus asks the audience to listen patiently as the play tells their tragic story.

key: macbeth.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE VIII.  Another part of the field.|1|1
summary: Macbeth refuses to kill himself and says he has avoided Macduff because he has already shed too much of his family’s blood. Macduff challenges him, and Macbeth boasts that no man born of a woman can harm him, but Macduff reveals that he was cut from his mother’s womb. Shaken and angry at the misleading prophecy, Macbeth refuses to fight, and Macduff demands that he surrender and face public humiliation.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|3|321
summary: Sampson denies insulting Abraham after Gregory warns him the law would not be on his side, but they argue over whose master is better and draw their swords. Benvolio tries to stop the fight, while Tybalt declares his hatred of peace, the Montagues, and Benvolio, and attacks him. A citizen calls for weapons and for both families to be beaten down, and Capulet asks about the noise.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|2|161
summary: Sampson boasts to Gregory that he will fight men and attack women, making a crude joke about cutting off their heads or taking their virginity. When two Montague men approach, Sampson draws his sword, and he and Gregory plan to provoke them into starting a fight so the law will favor them; Abraham challenges Sampson for biting his thumb at them.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|6|801
summary: Benvolio tells Lady Montague that more people joined the fight until the prince stopped it. Relieved that Romeo was not involved, she asks about him, and Benvolio says he saw Romeo early that morning but left him alone when Romeo avoided him. Montague says Romeo has often been seen crying and sighing outdoors before returning home to shut himself away.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|4|481
summary: Tybalt declares his hatred of peace and the Montagues and attacks Benvolio, while a citizen calls for weapons to stop the fighting. Capulet demands his sword, and Montague wants to confront him, but their wives discourage them. The Prince orders the fighters to drop their weapons, condemning the families for repeatedly disturbing Verona’s peace.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|8|1121
summary: Montague hopes Benvolio can discover why Romeo is unhappy and leaves with his wife. Benvolio asks Romeo about his sadness, and Romeo says the woman he loves does not return his feelings. Both lament how harsh love can be; Romeo also mentions a fight he has heard about and describes love as full of contradictions.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|1|1
summary: Sampson boasts to Gregory that he will fight the Montagues and push their men and women aside, while Gregory mocks his courage and reminds him that their masters’ quarrel is between men. Sampson says he will also be cruel to the women, joking that he will cut off their heads or take their virginity.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|5|641
summary: The Prince condemns Capulet and Montague’s repeated disturbances, threatens death for further fighting, and orders everyone away, telling Capulet to accompany him and Montague to meet him later. Benvolio tells Montague that their servants were fighting, he tried to separate them, and he fought Tybalt before others joined in; Lady Montague asks where Romeo is.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|7|961
summary: Montague tells Benvolio that his son Romeo sighs deeply, avoids daylight, and shuts himself in his room, and he fears Romeo’s sadness will lead to something terrible. Montague says Romeo will not reveal what troubles him, despite questions from friends and family; when Romeo approaches, Benvolio asks Montague to step aside so he can try to find out.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|10|1441
summary: Benvolio insists on accompanying Romeo and asks whom he loves. Romeo says he feels lost and admits he loves a beautiful woman, but she has vowed to remain chaste and rejects romantic words, admiring looks, and gifts. He laments that her beauty will die with her.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|11|1601
summary: Romeo tells Benvolio that the beautiful woman he loves has vowed to remain chaste, and he grieves that her beauty will die without being passed on to children. Benvolio advises him to look at other women, but Romeo says their beauty would only remind him of hers; Benvolio vows to teach him to forget her.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|9|1281
summary: Romeo describes love as a confusing mixture of opposites and says he feels its pain without feeling loved. Benvolio weeps for his cousin’s distress, but Romeo says that sympathy adds to his grief; when Romeo tries to leave, Benvolio insists on going with him and asks whom he loves.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A street.|1|1
summary: Capulet says that he and Montague are equally bound to keep the peace. Paris regrets their long conflict and asks again to marry Capulet’s daughter, Juliet. Capulet says Juliet is not yet fourteen and should wait two years, but invites Paris to win her affection and attend his feast, promising to respect her choice.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE I.  Verona. A public place.|12|1761
summary: Romeo tells Benvolio that even an exceptionally beautiful woman would only remind him of the woman he considers more beautiful. He says goodbye, insisting that Benvolio cannot teach him to forget her, but Benvolio promises to do so or remain forever in debt.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A street.|3|321
summary: A servant sent to find people on a written list cannot read their names and decides to seek help. Benvolio advises Romeo to ease his grief by finding a new love, but Romeo jokes about his advice and describes himself as imprisoned and tormented. The servant asks Romeo if he can read, and Romeo eventually assures him that he can.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A street.|4|481
summary: Romeo reads a list of guests for a servant, who explains that they are invited to supper at the wealthy Capulet’s house and invites Romeo to drink there, provided he is not a Montague. Benvolio tells Romeo that Rosaline, whom Romeo loves, will attend and urges him to compare her beauty with that of other women.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A street.|2|161
summary: Capulet welcomes Paris to his feast that night, promising the company of beautiful young women and encouraging him to consider them all, including Capulet’s daughter. Capulet gives a servant a list of guests to invite, and the servant puzzles over the task, comparing it to tradespeople using the wrong tools.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE II.  A street.|5|641
summary: Benvolio urges Romeo to attend Capulet’s feast and compare Rosaline with other beautiful women, confident that Romeo will find her less attractive. Romeo insists that no woman could be more beautiful and agrees to go only so that he can enjoy seeing Rosaline.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Capulet's house.|1|1
summary: Lady Capulet asks the Nurse to call Juliet and, after briefly sending the Nurse away, decides she may stay for their private talk. The Nurse says Juliet will turn fourteen on the eve of Lammas and remembers that her own daughter Susan, who has died, was the same age; she also recalls weaning Juliet eleven years ago.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Capulet's house.|2|161
summary: The Nurse recalls that Juliet will turn fourteen on the eve of Lammas, and that she weaned her eleven years ago by putting bitter wormwood on her nipple. She fondly remembers Juliet’s angry reaction, an earthquake that frightened her, and how her late husband joked after the toddler fell and hurt her forehead.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Capulet's house.|3|321
summary: The Nurse fondly recalls how her late husband joked that, although the young Juliet had fallen on her face, she would fall backward when she was older, and Juliet stopped crying and said yes. Lady Capulet and Juliet ask her to stop repeating the story. The Nurse praises Juliet as a beautiful baby and hopes to live to see her married.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Capulet's house.|4|481
summary: Juliet asks the Nurse to stop talking, and the Nurse blesses her and wishes to see her married. Lady Capulet asks Juliet about marriage and says that Paris wants her love; Juliet says she has not dreamed of marrying. The Nurse and Lady Capulet praise Paris, and Lady Capulet asks Juliet to consider him at the feast.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Capulet's house.|6|801
summary: Juliet tells Lady Capulet that she will look at the count with interest, but only as much as her mother permits. A servant announces that the guests have arrived and supper is ready, and urges them to follow; Lady Capulet says the count is waiting, while the Nurse wishes Juliet happy days and nights.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|1|1
summary: Romeo asks whether they should make a speech to excuse their entrance, but Benvolio dismisses the idea and says they will dance and leave. Romeo wants to carry a torch instead of dancing because love has weighed him down; Mercutio urges him to dance and calls love tender, while Romeo says it is rough.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE III.  A room in Capulet's house.|5|641
summary: Lady Capulet praises Paris’s beauty and wealth and asks whether Juliet could love him, urging her to look at him at the feast. The Nurse calls Paris a flower and jokes that men make women bigger; Juliet agrees to look at him but promises not to go beyond her mother’s wishes. A servant announces that the guests have arrived and supper is ready.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|2|161
summary: Romeo says love weighs him down and hurts him, but Mercutio jokes that Romeo should fight back and puts on a mask. Benvolio urges the men to enter and dance, while Romeo asks for a torch and says he will only watch; Mercutio urges him to stop dwelling on love and warns that they are wasting time.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|3|321
summary: Mercutio urges Romeo to get unstuck from love and stop wasting time, but Romeo doubts it is wise to go to the masquerade because he has had a dream. Mercutio says dreamers often lie, then describes Queen Mab, a tiny fairy who rides over sleepers’ noses in a delicate carriage drawn by tiny creatures.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|4|481
summary: Mercutio describes Queen Mab’s tiny fairy carriage, made from a hazelnut shell and delicate bits of insects and spiderwebs, and driven by a gnat. He says she brings people dreams of their desires: love, money, kisses, advancement, or war and drinking; she also punishes ladies whose breath smells of sweets with blisters on their lips.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  A hall in Capulet's house.|1|1
summary: The servants complain about the work of clearing the hall; one asks for a piece of almond cake to be saved and for Susan Grindstone and Nell to be let in. Capulet welcomes his guests, jokes that any woman who refuses to dance must have sore feet, remembers his own youthful flirting, and calls for music and room to dance.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|6|801
summary: Mercutio describes the wind turning from the frozen north toward the damp south, but Benvolio says their talk is delaying them and they will arrive late. Romeo fears that tonight’s festivities will set in motion events leading to his early death, but he trusts God to guide him and urges the others onward; Benvolio calls for the drum.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  A hall in Capulet's house.|4|481
summary: Tybalt angrily tells his uncle Capulet that Romeo, their Montague enemy, has come to insult their celebration. Capulet praises Romeo’s good reputation and orders Tybalt to leave him alone and look cheerful. When Tybalt refuses, Capulet angrily asserts his authority and scolds him for threatening to disrupt the feast.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|5|641
summary: Mercutio describes Queen Mab giving a sleeping soldier dreams of war, tangling horses’ and people’s hair, and pressing on sleeping young women. Romeo tells him to stop talking nonsense, and Mercutio agrees that dreams are insubstantial fantasies, more changeable than the wind. Benvolio warns that the conversation is distracting them and that they will arrive too late because supper is over.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  A hall in Capulet's house.|3|321
summary: Romeo asks a servant about Juliet, then praises her beauty and plans to approach her after the dance, convinced that he has never truly loved before. Recognizing Romeo’s voice, Tybalt angrily calls for his sword and says he would kill him for coming to mock the celebration; Capulet asks what is wrong, and Tybalt identifies Romeo as their enemy.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  A hall in Capulet's house.|5|641
summary: Capulet angrily orders Tybalt to be quiet and behave while welcoming his guests. Tybalt, trembling with restrained anger, decides to leave but vows that the intrusion will have bitter consequences. Romeo tells Juliet that he wants to kiss her, comparing her to a saint; she replies that pilgrims and saints touch hands and use their lips for prayer, but he asks her to grant his request.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  A hall in Capulet's house.|6|801
summary: Romeo and Juliet flirt by comparing their touches and kisses to a pilgrim’s prayers, and they kiss twice. The Nurse says Juliet’s mother wants her and reveals that Juliet is a wealthy Capulet, leaving Romeo distressed that he loves an enemy. Benvolio urges Romeo to leave, but Capulet asks the guests to stay for a small banquet.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|prologue|None|1|1
summary: The Chorus says that Romeo’s former desire has faded, and he and Juliet are now deeply in love, each captivated by the other’s looks. Because their families are enemies, Romeo cannot openly court Juliet, and she has even fewer opportunities to meet him, but their passion and time will help them overcome these difficulties.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  A lane by the wall of Capulet's orchard.|2|161
summary: Benvolio warns Mercutio that calling for Romeo may anger him, but Mercutio says he is only trying to summon him in his mistress’s name. Benvolio says Romeo is hiding among the trees, and Mercutio jokes about Romeo’s blind love and makes suggestive remarks about his mistress. Feeling cold and certain Romeo does not want to be found, they decide to leave.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|1|1
summary: Romeo says that people who have never been hurt make jokes about wounds. When Juliet appears at a window, he compares her to the sun and her eyes to stars, wishes she knew he loves her, and imagines that her eyes would shine so brightly in the sky that birds would think it was day.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  A hall in Capulet's house.|7|961
summary: Benvolio urges Romeo to leave, while Romeo worries about his feelings, and Capulet thanks his guests and prepares for bed. Juliet asks the Nurse about several young men, saying she will die unmarried if the one she loves is married. The Nurse identifies him as Romeo, a Montague and her family’s enemy; Juliet is distressed and tells the Nurse her words are a rhyme.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE I.  A lane by the wall of Capulet's orchard.|1|1
summary: Romeo turns back toward the Capulet orchard, saying his heart is there, while Benvolio and Mercutio look for him. Benvolio says Romeo climbed the orchard wall, and Mercutio mockingly tries to summon him with jokes about love and Rosaline’s body; when Benvolio warns that this may anger Romeo, Mercutio says his jokes are harmless and makes a more obscene comparison.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  A hall in Capulet's house.|8|1121
summary: Juliet is distressed that she has fallen in love with a hated enemy before discovering who he is. When the Nurse asks what she is saying, Juliet claims she learned the rhyme from someone she danced with; the Nurse then urges her to leave because the guests have gone.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|2|161
summary: Romeo admires Juliet’s beauty, compares her to stars and an angel, and wishes he could touch her cheek. Juliet laments Romeo’s family name and asks him to give it up or pledge his love so that she can give up hers, arguing that a name does not define a person. Romeo wonders whether to keep listening or speak.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT I|scene|SCENE V.  A hall in Capulet's house.|2|161
summary: Capulet recalls his younger days, welcomes his guests, and calls for music and dancing, then asks for more light and a cooler room. He and his cousin disagree about how many years have passed since they last wore masks at a celebration. Romeo asks a servant who a beautiful lady is; the servant does not know, and Romeo praises her radiance.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|3|321
summary: Juliet says Romeo’s family name is her enemy, not Romeo himself, and offers herself to him if he gives it up. Romeo agrees and says he hates his name because it is her enemy. Juliet recognizes his voice in the darkness, asks if he is Romeo Montague, and then asks how he came there.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|6|801
summary: Juliet tells Romeo that she could pretend to reject him so he will court her, but she would rather be honest. She asks him not to mistake her openness for shallow love, since he overheard her feelings. When Romeo begins to swear by the moon, Juliet warns that it is changeable; she loves him but fears their commitment is too sudden.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|8|1121
summary: Juliet tells Romeo that her love is endless, but the Nurse calls her inside; Romeo fears the night is too wonderful to be real. Juliet returns and asks him to send word of when and where they will marry if his intentions are honorable, or leave her alone if they are not. They say good night reluctantly, and Juliet calls Romeo back.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|4|481
summary: Juliet recognizes Romeo’s voice and asks how and why he entered the orchard, warning that her relatives will kill him if they find him. Romeo says love led him there and helped him get over the walls; he trusts the darkness to hide him and says he would rather die than live without Juliet’s love.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|5|641
summary: Romeo tells Juliet he would rather die from her family’s hatred than live without her love, and says love guided him to her and would lead him across the sea. Juliet admits she is embarrassed that he has heard her feelings and asks him to speak honestly about his love, worrying that he may think she has fallen for him too easily.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|7|961
summary: Juliet tells Romeo not to swear, saying that although she loves him, their commitment is too sudden, and she hopes their love will grow before they meet again. Romeo asks her to exchange vows, and Juliet says she has already pledged her boundless love; hearing her nurse call, she asks Romeo to remain faithful and wait.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|9|1281
summary: Juliet says good night to Romeo, then calls him back, wishing she could shout his name; Romeo delights in hearing her voice. They agree that she will send to him at nine the next morning, though she can hardly bear the wait. They linger because they love each other’s company, and Juliet wishes him to leave but remain close, like a pet bird.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|1|1
summary: Friar Laurence describes dawn driving away the darkness and says he must fill his basket with poisonous weeds and healing flowers. He reflects that the earth produces many different plants and receives them again in death, and that even good things can be misused: one flower cheers a person when smelled but kills when tasted.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|5|641
summary: Romeo asks Friar Laurence not to scold him for changing his love, explaining that the woman he loves now returns his affection, unlike Rosaline. The friar agrees to help Romeo, hoping the union will end the hatred between their families, but warns him to proceed carefully when Romeo wants to hurry.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|3|321
summary: Friar Laurence notes that Romeo has not been to bed and asks whether he was with Rosaline. Romeo says he has forgotten her and reveals that he and Capulet’s daughter love each other; he asks the friar to marry them that day. Friar Laurence is astonished that Romeo’s feelings have changed so quickly.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|2|161
summary: Friar Laurence reflects on good and evil, describing a flower that can both heal and kill and comparing its opposing powers to virtue and desire in humans. Romeo greets him early, and the friar suspects he has not slept. Romeo confirms this but denies having been with Rosaline, saying he has forgotten her and his sorrow over her.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|4|481
summary: Romeo tells Friar Laurence that he and Juliet have exchanged vows and asks the friar to marry them that day. Shocked that Romeo has so quickly abandoned his love for Rosaline, the friar mocks his recent tears and says he had warned Romeo against infatuation, not encouraged him to replace one love with another.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|1|1
summary: Mercutio asks where Romeo is, and Benvolio says he did not return to his father’s house and that Tybalt has sent him a letter. Mercutio assumes it is a challenge, and Benvolio expects Romeo to accept it. Mercutio jokes that Romeo is already undone by his love for Rosaline and doubts he can face Tybalt, a skilled and precise duelist.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|10|1441
summary: Romeo says he would stay with Juliet and forget his home, while Juliet wants him to leave because morning is near but wishes she could keep him close like a pet bird. Romeo wishes he were her bird, and Juliet says she would love him to death, then bids him good night. Romeo wishes her peaceful sleep and decides to seek his spiritual father’s help and share his happiness.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|3|321
summary: Mercutio mocks several famous women, then greets Romeo and jokes that he slipped away from his friends the previous night. Romeo excuses himself, and the two trade increasingly elaborate puns until Mercutio jokingly asks Benvolio to step between them because his wit is failing.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|4|481
summary: Romeo and Mercutio trade playful jokes and insults, with Mercutio asking Benvolio to come between them when he feels his wit failing. Mercutio threatens to bite Romeo’s ear after being called a goose, but praises him for being sociable again instead of groaning about love.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|5|641
summary: Mercutio tells Romeo that joking makes him better company than groaning over love, then trades crude jokes with Benvolio, who asks him to stop. The Nurse arrives with Peter and asks for her fan; Mercutio mocks her appearance and makes a crude joke about the time, prompting her protest. Romeo describes Mercutio as a man made by God to ruin himself.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|2|161
summary: Mercutio mocks an overly fashionable duelist, imitating his fencing terms and affected speech, while Benvolio asks what he means. When Benvolio announces Romeo’s arrival, Mercutio jokes that Romeo is thin and lovesick, exaggerates the beauty of the woman he loves, and greets him in French while teasing him about his clothes.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|7|961
summary: Mercutio sings, invites Romeo to dinner at his father’s house, and mockingly bids the Nurse farewell. Romeo agrees to follow him and tells the Nurse that Mercutio talks more than he is willing to stand behind. The angry Nurse threatens Mercutio and scolds Peter for not defending her, but Peter says he would have drawn his weapon if he had seen a good reason.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|6|801
summary: Mercutio makes a crude joke about noon, and the Nurse rebukes him before asking where she can find Romeo. Romeo playfully identifies himself, and the Nurse asks to speak privately with him. Benvolio jokes about a supper invitation, while Mercutio calls her a madam and sings a mocking song about an old hare.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|9|1281
summary: The Nurse says Juliet will be delighted by Romeo’s offer, and Romeo asks her to tell Juliet to come to Friar Laurence’s cell that afternoon for confession and marriage. He offers the Nurse money and says his servant will bring her a rope ladder for his secret visit that night; when she asks if the servant can keep a secret, Romeo assures her he can.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|8|1121
summary: Peter tells the Nurse that he saw no one insult her, but would have drawn his sword if he had seen a lawful reason to fight. Still furious, the Nurse warns Romeo not to deceive Juliet, and when Romeo begins to send Juliet a message, she eagerly interrupts, saying Juliet will be delighted; Romeo points out that she is not listening.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE IV.  A street.|10|1441
summary: The Nurse asks whether Romeo’s servant can keep a secret, and Romeo assures her he can. She praises Juliet, says she dislikes Paris, and describes teasing her about him and her fond remarks about Romeo and rosemary. Romeo asks the Nurse to greet Juliet for him; after he leaves, she tells Peter to take her fan and hurry ahead.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|1|1
summary: Juliet impatiently complains that the Nurse has been gone for three hours, though she promised to return in half an hour with news of Romeo. When the Nurse arrives with Peter, Juliet asks her to send him away and anxiously begs for news, troubled by the Nurse’s sad expression.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|2|161
summary: Juliet anxiously begs the Nurse to say whether her news is good or bad, but the Nurse complains that she is tired and out of breath. Impatient with the delay, Juliet presses her for an answer; the Nurse says Juliet has chosen poorly, then praises Romeo’s face and legs.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|4|481
summary: Juliet impatiently asks the Nurse for Romeo’s message, but the Nurse praises him, asks about Juliet’s mother, and complains about her aching bones. The Nurse finally tells Juliet to go to Friar Laurence, where Romeo waits to marry her, and says she will fetch a ladder for Romeo to climb that night. Juliet happily hurries away.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE VI.  Friar Laurence's cell.|1|1
summary: Friar Laurence hopes the marriage will bring no sorrow, but warns Romeo that intense love can end violently and advises him to love moderately. Romeo says seeing Juliet brings him more joy than any sorrow could outweigh and asks the friar to marry them. Juliet enters and greets the friar, and Romeo asks her to describe her joy if it matches his.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|3|321
summary: The Nurse praises Romeo’s looks and gentle nature, then complains of a headache and back pain and blames Juliet for sending her out. Juliet says she is sorry the Nurse feels unwell and eagerly asks what Romeo says about their marriage. Instead of answering, the Nurse praises him again and asks where Juliet’s mother is, surprising Juliet.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A public place.|1|1
summary: Benvolio asks Mercutio to leave because the day is hot, the Capulets are out, and a meeting with them could lead to a fight. Mercutio teases Benvolio for being quick-tempered, comparing him to a man who draws his sword after drinking and joking that he would quarrel over the smallest differences.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT II|scene|SCENE VI.  Friar Laurence's cell.|2|161
summary: Friar Laurence tells Juliet that Romeo will thank her for them both, and she says she owes Romeo just as much. Romeo asks Juliet to express their shared joy, but she says her love is too great to measure. The friar asks them to come with him, saying they cannot be alone together until the church joins them in marriage.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A public place.|2|161
summary: Mercutio teases Benvolio for supposedly starting fights over ridiculous things, while Benvolio says Mercutio is so quarrelsome that his life cannot be worth much. When Benvolio spots the approaching Capulets, Mercutio says he does not care. Tybalt asks to speak with one of them, and Mercutio challenges him to add a blow to his words; Tybalt agrees.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A public place.|3|321
summary: Tybalt approaches Mercutio and asks to speak with him, but Mercutio provokes him and threatens him with his sword. Benvolio urges them to settle their grievances privately or leave, but Mercutio refuses to move. When Romeo arrives, Mercutio mocks Tybalt’s claim that Romeo is his man, and Tybalt calls Romeo a villain.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A public place.|6|801
summary: Mercutio curses both families, blames Romeo for coming between him and Tybalt, and asks Benvolio to help him find shelter. Romeo mourns his friend’s mortal wound and says his love for Juliet has softened his courage. Benvolio announces Mercutio’s death and Tybalt’s return, and Romeo, fearing more sorrow, decides to abandon restraint and give way to fury.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A public place.|4|481
