summary: Tybalt calls Romeo a villain and demands that he draw his sword, but Romeo denies having injured him and says he loves Tybalt for a reason Tybalt does not yet understand. Angry at Romeo’s peaceful response, Mercutio draws his own sword, mocks Tybalt as a king of cats, and challenges him to fight.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A public place.|7|961
summary: Romeo predicts more trouble and, furious that Tybalt killed Mercutio, challenges Tybalt; they fight, and Tybalt is killed. Benvolio urges Romeo to flee before the prince sentences him to death, and Romeo laments his fate. A citizen demands to know where Tybalt is, and Benvolio tells the prince that Romeo killed him.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A public place.|8|1121
summary: The Prince asks who started the deadly fight, and Benvolio says Romeo killed Tybalt after Tybalt killed Mercutio. Lady Capulet mourns Tybalt and demands a Montague’s blood in revenge. Benvolio explains that Romeo had tried to calm Tybalt, but Tybalt attacked Mercutio, and Romeo intervened to stop their fight.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A public place.|5|641
summary: Mercutio challenges Tybalt to fight, while Romeo urges them to stop and asks Benvolio to knock down their weapons, reminding them that the prince has forbidden street fights. Mercutio is wounded and asks his page to fetch a surgeon. Despite Romeo’s reassurance, Mercutio says the wound is fatal, curses both families, and bitterly insults Tybalt.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A public place.|9|1281
summary: Benvolio describes how Romeo tried to stop Mercutio and Tybalt from fighting, but Tybalt struck Mercutio under Romeo’s arm and fled. Tybalt returned, and Romeo killed him in revenge before running away. Lady Capulet accuses Benvolio of lying and demands Romeo’s execution, but Montague argues that Romeo only did what the law would have done to Tybalt.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|1|1
summary: Juliet impatiently calls for the sun to set and night to come, so Romeo can join her unseen. She longs to make love with him but hopes darkness will hide her blushes until she feels less shy. She imagines that, when Romeo dies, he could become stars so beautiful that the world would love night more than the sun.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE I.  A public place.|10|1441
summary: Lady Capulet insists that Romeo must die, but Montague argues that Romeo was Mercutio’s friend and killed Tybalt only after Tybalt killed Mercutio. The Prince exiles Romeo and declares that he will be killed if found, fines the feuding families for the loss of his own relative, refuses to hear pleas, and orders the body removed.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|6|801
summary: Juliet tells herself to stop crying because her husband Romeo is alive, while Tybalt, who would have killed him, is dead. But she says Romeo’s banishment is a grief beyond measure, worse than Tybalt’s death or the loss of her parents. She asks where her parents are, and the Nurse says they are weeping and wailing.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|2|161
summary: Juliet imagines Romeo as stars beautifying the night and impatiently awaits their time together. The Nurse arrives with cords Romeo requested, but wrings her hands and cries that someone is dead. Confused and distressed by the Nurse’s mention of Romeo, Juliet asks whether he has killed himself.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|3|321
summary: The Nurse cries out about Romeo, and Juliet, fearing he has killed himself, begs for a clear answer. The Nurse describes seeing a pale, bloody corpse, and Juliet, believing Romeo is dead, wishes to die and lie beside him. When the Nurse mourns Tybalt by name, Juliet is confused and asks whether Romeo has been killed.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|4|481
summary: The Nurse mourns Tybalt, and Juliet fears that both her cousin and her beloved Romeo are dead. When the Nurse explains that Romeo killed Tybalt and has been banished, Juliet is shocked and condemns him as a monster hidden behind a beautiful face, while the Nurse declares that men cannot be trusted.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|5|641
summary: Juliet laments that someone as beautiful as Romeo could conceal such evil. The Nurse declares that men cannot be trusted and curses Romeo, but Juliet rebukes her and regrets criticizing her husband. When the Nurse reminds her that Romeo killed her cousin Tybalt, Juliet struggles with her grief but takes comfort that Romeo is alive, since Tybalt would have killed him.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|1|1
summary: Friar Laurence tells a fearful Romeo that the prince has banished him from Verona rather than sentencing him to death. Romeo is horrified, saying that life outside Verona would be torture and that banishment is worse than death. Friar Laurence calls him ungrateful and insists that the prince’s sentence is merciful.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|2|161
summary: Friar Laurence scolds Romeo for being ungrateful, saying the prince has shown mercy by sentencing him to banishment rather than death. Romeo insists that exile is torture because he cannot see Juliet, while even animals and flies can approach her; he asks why the friar did not use poison or a knife instead of the deadly word “banished.”

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE II.  Capulet's orchard.|7|961
summary: Juliet grieves over Romeo’s banishment and asks where her parents are; the Nurse says they are mourning Tybalt. Juliet laments that Romeo will not use the ropes to reach her bed and expects to die a virgin without him. The Nurse promises to find Romeo at Laurence’s cell, and Juliet asks her to give him a ring and bring him for a final farewell.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|4|481
summary: Romeo lies on the ground in despair, saying Friar Laurence cannot understand his grief over Juliet, Tybalt’s death, and his banishment. When someone knocks, the friar urges Romeo to hide, but Juliet’s nurse enters and asks for him. Seeing Romeo in tears, she says Juliet is also lying and weeping, and urges him to stand up for her sake.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|5|641
summary: The Nurse tells Romeo that Juliet is weeping, calling out for Tybalt and Romeo, and repeatedly falling onto her bed. Romeo fears Juliet sees him as a murderer because he killed her relative, Tybalt; blaming his own name for her suffering, he asks Friar Laurence where it is lodged in his body so he can destroy it, and the friar stops him.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|6|801
summary: Romeo curses his name because he believes it killed Juliet’s kinsman Tybalt, and asks Friar Laurence where it lives in his body so he can destroy it. The friar stops Romeo from harming himself, rebukes his despair and fury, and warns that killing himself would also harm Juliet and betray his love for her.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|3|321
summary: Romeo tells Friar Laurence that banishment feels like a death sentence, and he rejects the friar’s offer of philosophical comfort because it cannot create another Juliet or reverse the prince’s ruling. He says the friar cannot understand his suffering unless he too were young, newly married, responsible for Tybalt’s death, and banished; Romeo falls to the ground in despair.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|8|1121
summary: Friar Laurence warns Romeo against despair and tells him to comfort Juliet, then leave for Mantua before the watch begins, while they work to reveal the marriage, reconcile their families, and win the prince’s pardon. The Nurse praises the friar’s advice and promises to tell Juliet that Romeo is coming; she gives Romeo a ring from Juliet, which cheers him.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  A room in Capulet's house.|1|1
summary: Capulet tells Paris that Juliet is grieving for her cousin Tybalt and will not come downstairs, while Paris says it is no time for courtship. Confident that Juliet will obey him, Capulet tells Lady Capulet to inform her of Paris’s love and arrange their marriage for Thursday, with only a few friends present.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|1|1
summary: Juliet urges Romeo to stay, insisting that the bird they heard was a nightingale and that the light is not from the rising sun. Romeo says it is morning and that he must leave for Mantua or die, but then agrees to stay, accepting the risk of death because Juliet wants him to.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|7|961
summary: Friar Laurence scolds Romeo for misusing his courage, love, and intelligence and for despairing despite his good fortune. He reminds Romeo that Juliet is alive, that Romeo killed Tybalt rather than being killed, and that he has been exiled instead of sentenced to death. He tells Romeo to visit and comfort Juliet, but to leave before the night watch is posted.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE III.  Friar Laurence's cell.|9|1281
summary: The Nurse urges Romeo to hurry because it is late, and Romeo says he feels comforted. Friar Laurence tells him to leave before the watch is set or depart in disguise at dawn, then stay in Mantua; he will find Romeo’s servant to send him good news. Romeo says he is sorry to leave the friar so quickly, but a greater joy calls him away.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE IV.  A room in Capulet's house.|2|161
summary: Capulet decides that Juliet will marry Paris on Thursday and plans a small wedding, since a large celebration so soon after Tybalt’s death would seem disrespectful. Paris wishes Thursday were tomorrow, and Capulet tells his wife to prepare Juliet for the wedding before saying good night.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|2|161
summary: Romeo insists it is not yet day and says he would rather stay with Juliet, even if it means death. Juliet recognizes the lark’s song and urges him to leave, while both lament their separation. The Nurse warns that Juliet’s mother is coming, and Romeo says goodbye and plans to climb down after a kiss; Juliet asks to hear from him every hour.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|5|641
summary: Lady Capulet calls Romeo a villain for killing Tybalt and promises Juliet that she will send someone to poison him in Mantua. Juliet privately rejects the description of Romeo as a villain, but tells her mother she wants revenge and offers to prepare the poison, while hinting at her love for Romeo and her sorrow at being separated from him.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|9|1281
summary: Juliet begs her father to hear her, but Capulet angrily orders her to go to church on Thursday or never see him again, calling her a curse. Lady Capulet says he is too angry, and the Nurse defends Juliet, but Capulet silences her and says he has worked tirelessly to find Juliet a husband of noble birth and wealth.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|3|321
summary: After the Nurse warns them to be careful, Romeo and Juliet exchange a farewell kiss, and he descends from her window. Juliet fears they may never meet again and thinks Romeo looks like a dead man, but he promises to send messages and believes they will reunite. Juliet begs fickle fortune to bring him back, then hears Lady Capulet calling her.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|4|481
summary: Juliet asks fickle Fortune to send the faithful Romeo back, then wonders why her mother has come at such an unusual hour. Lady Capulet tells Juliet to stop weeping for her dead cousin and suggests she is really upset because his killer, Romeo, is still alive. Juliet privately rejects her mother’s description of Romeo as a villain and says she forgives him.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|6|801
summary: Juliet says she hates hearing Romeo’s name and wishes she could avenge her cousin’s death on him. Lady Capulet offers to find someone to do it, then announces that Juliet’s father has arranged for her to marry Paris on Thursday. Juliet objects to the rushed marriage and says she would rather marry Romeo.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|8|1121
summary: Lady Capulet tells her husband that Juliet refuses the marriage and says she wishes Juliet were dead. Juliet says she is grateful for her parents’ loving intention but cannot be proud of a match she hates. Furious, Capulet insults her and threatens to drag her to church to marry Paris on Thursday; Lady Capulet protests, and Juliet kneels and begs him to listen.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|7|961
summary: Juliet tells Lady Capulet that she will not marry yet and would rather marry Romeo, whom she claims to hate, than Paris. Capulet arrives, compares Juliet’s tears and sighs to a storm at sea, and asks whether she has been told of their decision. Lady Capulet says Juliet refuses and wishes her dead, leaving Capulet astonished.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|11|1601
summary: Capulet tells Juliet that his wealth will never benefit her and that he will not go back on his word. Grieving, Juliet begs her mother to delay the marriage or place her in Tybalt’s tomb, but Lady Capulet refuses to help. Juliet asks the Nurse for comfort, and the Nurse advises her to marry the count because Romeo is banished and unlikely to return openly.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|10|1441
summary: Lady Capulet says Capulet is too angry, but he rages that Juliet refuses the wealthy, well-born husband he has chosen for her. He threatens to disown her and leave her to starve if she will not marry on Thursday; Juliet appeals to heaven for pity and begs her mother not to abandon her and to delay the marriage.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|12|1761
summary: The Nurse says Romeo cannot return openly and urges Juliet to marry Paris, whom she praises as far better than Romeo. Juliet asks whether she means it, then tells her to inform Lady Capulet that she is going to Friar Laurence for confession. After the Nurse leaves, Juliet angrily condemns her for urging her to break her marriage vow and criticizing Romeo after praising him so often.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  Friar Laurence's cell.|2|161
summary: Paris speaks of Thursday and asks whether Juliet has come to confess to Friar Laurence. Juliet gives evasive answers about loving Paris and speaks sadly about her tear-stained face. Friar Laurence agrees to speak with Juliet alone, and Paris says he will wake her early on Thursday before saying goodbye with a kiss.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  Friar Laurence's cell.|1|1
summary: Paris tells Friar Laurence that Juliet’s father has hurried their wedding to Thursday, hoping marriage will distract her from grieving for Tybalt. The friar is uneasy because Paris does not know how Juliet feels and privately wishes he had no reason to delay the marriage. When Juliet arrives, Paris calls her his future wife, but she answers him cautiously.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT III|scene|SCENE V.  Capulet's orchard.|13|1921
summary: After the Nurse says something is wisely done, Juliet angrily calls her wicked for urging her to break her promise and for criticizing the husband she has praised so often. Juliet decides not to confide in the Nurse again and to seek the friar’s help; if all else fails, she can kill herself.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  Friar Laurence's cell.|4|481
summary: Juliet asks Friar Laurence for immediate advice, threatening to kill herself rather than betray her love and marry Paris. The friar offers hope through a desperate, deathlike remedy, and Juliet declares that she would face falls, thieves, snakes, bears, or a house full of human bones rather than marry Paris.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  Friar Laurence's cell.|3|321
summary: Friar Laurence asks Paris to leave him alone with Juliet, and Paris kisses her goodbye, promising to wake her early on Thursday. Juliet begs the friar to weep with her and find a way to prevent her marriage to Paris. She says she is already married to Romeo and will kill herself with a knife rather than betray him, unless the friar can help.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  Friar Laurence's cell.|5|641
summary: Juliet says she will face snakes, bears, graves, and human remains without fear to remain faithful to Romeo. Friar Laurence tells her to agree to marry Paris, then sleep alone the next night and drink a liquid that will make her appear dead.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  Friar Laurence's cell.|7|961
summary: Friar Laurence gives Juliet something he says will free her from her present shame, urging her not to let fear weaken her resolve. Juliet eagerly accepts it and dismisses her fear; the friar promises to send a messenger with letters to her husband in Mantua, and Juliet asks love to give her strength before saying goodbye.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE II.  Hall in Capulet's house.|3|321
summary: Capulet says he will stay up all night and take charge of the household preparations. Finding that everyone is out, he decides to go to Count Paris himself to prepare him for the next day, and says he feels delighted that his rebellious daughter Juliet has become obedient.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE II.  Hall in Capulet's house.|1|1
summary: Capulet orders servants to invite guests and hire twenty skilled cooks, and one servant jokes about testing whether the cooks can lick their fingers. Capulet worries about the preparations and complains that Juliet is stubborn, but she returns from Friar Laurence, begs her father’s forgiveness, and promises to obey him. Delighted, Capulet orders the wedding to Paris for the next morning; Juliet says she has met Paris and treated him affectionately within proper bounds.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE II.  Hall in Capulet's house.|2|161
summary: Capulet decides that Juliet will marry Paris tomorrow, and Juliet says she met Paris at Friar Laurence’s cell and treated him affectionately but modestly. Juliet asks the Nurse to help choose her wedding clothes, while Lady Capulet worries there is too little time; Capulet promises to oversee the preparations and says he will go to Paris himself.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  Juliet's chamber.|1|1
summary: Juliet asks the Nurse and Lady Capulet to leave her alone, saying she needs to pray, and Lady Capulet wishes her good night. Frightened, Juliet briefly considers calling the Nurse back but decides she must face her ordeal alone. She worries that the potion may not work and places a dagger nearby to prevent her marriage; she also fears the friar may have given her poison.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE I.  Friar Laurence's cell.|6|801
summary: Friar Laurence tells Juliet she will appear dead for forty-two hours and be carried to the Capulet tomb after her bridegroom finds her. He will summon Romeo, who will take her to Mantua when she wakes, freeing her from her predicament. Juliet eagerly asks for the remedy and insists she is not afraid; the friar gives it to her and urges her to be brave.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  Juliet's chamber.|3|321
summary: Juliet fears that if she wakes in her family’s tomb, the smells, imagined screams, and sight of her ancestors’ bones and Tybalt’s decaying body will drive her mad and make her kill herself with a bone. She imagines Tybalt’s ghost pursuing Romeo, who killed him, and begs it to stop before drinking to Romeo.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE III.  Juliet's chamber.|2|161
summary: Juliet fears the mixture may fail to stop her wedding and places a dagger nearby. She also wonders whether the friar has poisoned her to hide his role in her marriage to Romeo, although she believes him to be holy. She fears waking in the tomb before Romeo arrives, suffocating or being terrified by her ancestors’ bones, Tybalt’s decaying body, and spirits.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE IV.  Hall in Capulet's house.|1|1
summary: Lady Capulet and the Nurse prepare food, while Capulet urges everyone to hurry and spare no expense. The Nurse tells Capulet to go to bed, and Lady Capulet teases him about his past pursuit of women. Capulet jokes with a servant sent to fetch dry logs, then says that the Count will soon arrive with music, which he thinks he can hear.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Juliet's chamber.|2|161
summary: Lady Capulet begs Juliet to wake, and the Nurse declares her dead. Capulet finds Juliet cold and stiff, mourns her as a flower destroyed by frost, and tells Friar Laurence that Death has claimed her instead of her bridegroom. Paris is shocked to find Juliet apparently dead on their wedding morning, while Lady Capulet laments the miserable day.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE IV.  Hall in Capulet's house.|2|161
summary: The Second Servant says there is no need to trouble Peter, and Capulet jokingly calls the servant a fool. Hearing music and realizing that Paris has arrived, Capulet calls for the Nurse and his wife, urgently tells the Nurse to wake and dress Juliet, and says he will go talk to Paris.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Juliet's chamber.|1|1
summary: The Nurse tries to wake Juliet, joking that her marriage to Paris will leave her little sleep, but finds her apparently dead and calls for help. Lady Capulet is devastated and begs her daughter to revive, while Capulet asks for Juliet to be brought to her bridegroom and is told that she is dead.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Juliet's chamber.|4|481
summary: Capulet mourns Juliet, saying that his joy is buried with her. Friar Laurence urges the family to stop grieving, saying that Juliet is better off in heaven, and tells them to dress her body, place rosemary on it, and carry it to church. Capulet says their preparations for a celebration must now serve a funeral.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Juliet's chamber.|3|321
summary: Capulet, Lady Capulet, the Nurse, and Paris mourn Juliet, whom they believe is dead, calling the day cruel and miserable. Lady Capulet grieves for her only child, Paris laments the loss of his love, and Capulet says his joy has died with his daughter. Friar Laurence tells them to be quiet, saying their outbursts will not ease their distress.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Juliet's chamber.|5|641
summary: Friar Laurence tells the mourners to dress Juliet in her finest clothes and prepare to carry her to the grave, urging them to accept heaven’s will. Capulet sadly describes how the wedding preparations must become funeral arrangements. After the Nurse calls the situation pitiful, Peter asks the musicians to play a cheerful tune to comfort him, but they refuse.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Juliet's chamber.|7|961
summary: Peter asks three musicians why a song calls music’s sound “silver.” Two suggest that silver sounds sweet and that musicians play for silver money; the third cannot answer, so Peter jokes that musicians earn no gold. Annoyed by Peter, the musicians decide to wait inside for the mourners and dinner.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT IV|scene|SCENE V.  Juliet's chamber.|6|801
summary: Peter asks the musicians to play a cheerful tune to comfort his sorrow, but the first musician says it is not the time for music. After trading insults and threats with him, Peter agrees to put away his dagger and challenges the musicians to explain why a song describes music as having a “silver sound.” One says silver sounds sweet, and Peter asks Hugh Rebeck for his answer.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  Mantua. A street.|4|481
summary: Romeo asks the apothecary for a fast-acting poison, but the apothecary says selling it is punishable by death. Romeo urges him to break the law because he is desperately poor, and the apothecary reluctantly agrees. After receiving instructions, Romeo pays him, calls gold a worse poison, and tells him to buy food.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  Mantua. A street.|2|161
summary: Balthasar apologizes for bringing Romeo the news that Juliet lies in her family’s vault. Romeo defies the stars and orders ink, paper, and horses, dismissing Balthasar’s concern about his wild appearance and learning that no letter has arrived from the friar. Desperate to lie with Juliet that night, Romeo remembers a nearby apothecary who looks desperately poor.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  Mantua. A street.|3|321
summary: Romeo recalls a painfully thin, impoverished apothecary whose shop was filled with strange animal remains and almost empty shelves. Believing the man’s poverty will make him sell poison despite the death penalty for doing so, Romeo calls him out of his closed shop and offers him forty ducats for a fast-acting poison.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  Mantua. A street.|1|1
summary: Romeo happily describes a dream in which Juliet finds him dead, revives him with kisses, and he becomes an emperor; he hopes the dream promises good news. Balthasar arrives from Verona and apologetically tells Romeo that he saw Juliet laid in her family’s tomb. Romeo reacts by defying the stars.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  Friar Laurence's cell.|1|1
summary: Friar John tells Friar Laurence that officials quarantined him on suspicion of plague, preventing him from delivering Laurence’s letter to Romeo or sending word. Alarmed because the letter contained important news, Laurence asks John for a crowbar and decides to go alone to Juliet’s tomb, where she will wake within three hours. He expects her to blame him because Romeo has not been informed.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE I.  Mantua. A street.|5|641
summary: Romeo tells the apothecary that the gold he gives him is more poisonous to human souls and causes more murders than the drugs the apothecary is forbidden to sell. He urges the man to buy food and gain weight, then takes the poison to Juliet’s grave, where he plans to use it.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|1|1
summary: Paris tells his page to put out the torch, hide, and warn him if anyone approaches; the page is afraid but agrees. Paris scatters flowers on Juliet’s grave and mourns her, promising to return nightly to weep. When the page whistles, Paris hides, and Romeo arrives, asking for tools and giving someone a letter to deliver to his father.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE II.  Friar Laurence's cell.|2|161
summary: Friar John agrees to go and bring Friar Laurence what he has requested. Laurence says he must go alone to Juliet’s tomb, where she will wake within three hours; he expects her to blame him for not informing Romeo, so he plans to write to Romeo in Mantua and shelter her until he arrives.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|3|321
summary: Romeo bids Balthasar farewell, but Balthasar hides nearby because he fears Romeo’s intentions. Romeo forces open the Capulet tomb, while Paris, believing he intends to desecrate the bodies, confronts him and tries to arrest him. Romeo says he has come to die and begs Paris to leave rather than provoke a desperate man to violence.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|4|481
summary: Romeo begs Paris to leave, warning that he is armed against himself and does not want to harm him. Paris refuses and tries to arrest him, so they fight as the page runs to call the watch. Mortally wounded, Paris asks to be laid beside Juliet; Romeo agrees, recognizes him, and mourns their shared misfortune.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|2|161
summary: Paris, mourning his love, sees a torch and hides in the darkness. Romeo asks Balthasar for tools and orders him to deliver a letter to his father, saying he intends to see his lady’s face and take a ring from her finger. Romeo threatens to tear Balthasar apart if he interferes, but Balthasar secretly decides to stay nearby because Romeo’s appearance frightens him.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|7|961
summary: Romeo praises the apothecary’s fast-acting poison and dies with a kiss. Friar Laurence arrives at the churchyard, where Balthasar tells him that Romeo is in the Capulet tomb and has threatened to kill him if he stays to watch. Balthasar describes a dream of Romeo killing someone, and the frightened friar finds blood and abandoned swords near the tomb.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|8|1121
summary: Balthasar says that Romeo fought and killed another man, and Friar Laurence finds Romeo and Paris dead in the tomb. Juliet wakes and asks for Romeo; the friar urges her to leave and offers to place her with nuns, but she refuses. After he leaves, Juliet finds a cup in Romeo’s hand and realizes he has taken all the poison.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|5|641
summary: Romeo lays Paris in the Capulet tomb, calling him a fellow victim of misfortune, and says Juliet’s beauty fills the grave with light. He marvels that Juliet still looks beautiful despite her apparent death, asks Tybalt’s forgiveness, and wonders whether he can honor Tybalt by killing himself, the man who killed him.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|9|1281
summary: Friar Laurence leaves when Juliet refuses to go with him. Finding that Romeo has died from poison, Juliet kisses him, hoping to die too, then hears someone approaching and stabs herself with his dagger. The watchmen find Juliet and the slain count, send for the prince and both families, and detain Romeo’s servant.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|6|801
summary: Romeo asks his cousin’s forgiveness and marvels that Juliet is still beautiful, imagining that death wants her as a lover. Determined to remain with her, he embraces and kisses her, drinks poison, and dies. Friar Laurence stumbles among the graves and calls out; Balthasar answers that he is a friend who knows him well.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|10|1441
summary: The watchmen find Romeo’s servant and a trembling, weeping friar carrying grave-opening tools, and hold them for the Prince. The Prince and the Capulets arrive amid cries about Romeo, Juliet, and Paris; a watchman reports that all three are dead, with Juliet newly killed. The Prince orders an investigation, while Capulet is horrified to see his daughter bleeding from a dagger wound.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|12|1761
summary: The Prince calls for the suspects and asks Friar Laurence what he knows. The friar explains that he secretly married Romeo and Juliet, and that Romeo was banished after Tybalt’s death, leaving Juliet grieving for him. When her family planned to force her to marry Paris, Juliet threatened to kill herself, so the friar gave her a sleeping potion that worked as intended.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|11|1601
summary: The watchman reports finding a friar and Romeo’s dead servant with tools for opening tombs. Capulet and his wife grieve over Juliet’s body and the dagger in her chest; Montague says his wife died grieving over Romeo’s exile and mourns his son. The Prince urges patience until the deaths can be investigated, and Friar Laurence says he is the most suspected.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|13|1921
summary: Friar Laurence explains that Juliet threatened to kill herself rather than enter a second marriage, so he gave her a potion to make her appear dead and sent word to Romeo, but the letter never arrived. He came to the tomb to collect her and found Romeo and Paris dead. Juliet woke but refused to leave with him; a noise frightened him away, and she apparently killed herself.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|14|2081
summary: Friar Laurence says a noise scared him away from Juliet’s tomb, and she refused to leave and apparently killed herself; he offers his life if he is at fault. The Prince calls him holy and questions Balthasar, who says he brought Romeo news of Juliet’s death and was threatened into leaving him at the tomb. Paris’s page says Paris came to scatter flowers on Juliet’s grave.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|16|2401
summary: Montague promises to raise a pure gold statue of faithful Juliet, and Capulet promises an equally rich statue of Romeo beside hers, mourning the lovers as victims of their families’ hatred. The Prince calls the morning’s peace gloomy and says they must discuss the tragedy further; some people will be pardoned and others punished.

key: romeo_and_juliet.xml|ACT V|scene|SCENE III.  A churchyard; in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.|15|2241
summary: The page tells the Prince that his master brought flowers to his lady’s grave and drew his sword on a man opening the tomb, so he ran for help. The Prince says Romeo’s letter confirms the friar’s account and blames the families’ hatred and his own tolerance of it for their losses. Capulet and Montague reconcile and promise rich statues of Juliet and Romeo.
